domain: Section 2: Planning and implementing a cloud solution

questions.title: Legacy app needing kernel-level control
questions.summary: Only Compute Engine gives OS-level control; managed container platforms abstract the kernel away.
questions.question: Orrin Labs runs a licensed spectroscopy package that loads its own kernel module at boot, checks a licence tied to a fixed MAC address, and needs root access to the operating system to install vendor patches. The team wants to move it to Google Cloud without changing the software. Which compute platform should you choose?

options.A: Google Kubernetes Engine
options.B: Compute Engine virtual machines
options.C: Cloud Run
options.D: Cloud Run functions

explanation.summary: Only Compute Engine gives OS-level control and persistent VM identity; every managed container platform abstracts the kernel away.

option_breakdown.A: Containers share the node's kernel, and GKE manages the node images, so the app gets neither its own kernel module nor root on the OS.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Only Compute Engine gives OS-level control and root on your own VM; every managed container platform abstracts the kernel away.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Run runs containers in a sandbox with no access to the host kernel or OS.
option_breakdown.D: Functions run your code in a managed runtime with no OS access at all.

questions.title: Forty interdependent microservices
questions.summary: A fleet of interdependent services with shared lifecycle policy is what Kubernetes orchestration exists for.
questions.question: Forty microservices, several of them stateful with persistent volumes, are deployed today with Kubernetes manifests. The team wants per-service autoscaling, rolling updates and one operational model in two regions, without managing a control plane. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: Cloud Run functions
options.B: Cloud Run services
options.C: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
options.D: Compute Engine managed instance groups

explanation.summary: GKE runs the existing Kubernetes manifests, including StatefulSets with persistent volumes, on a control plane Google manages.

option_breakdown.A: Functions are single-purpose handlers; they don't run Kubernetes manifests or stateful services.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Run services are stateless and can't run StatefulSets with persistent volumes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. GKE runs the manifests unchanged, including stateful workloads, with per-service autoscaling and rolling updates.
option_breakdown.D: VMs would mean rebuilding the orchestration that Kubernetes already provides.

questions.title: Spiky stateless API with no cluster to run
questions.summary: Cloud Run autoscales a container on request concurrency and scales to zero with no cluster.
questions.question: A stateless HTTPS API packaged as a container image has spiky traffic and must scale to zero overnight. The team does not want to manage VMs or a Kubernetes cluster. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: Compute Engine virtual machines
options.B: Google Kubernetes Engine
options.C: Cloud Run functions
options.D: Cloud Run

explanation.summary: Cloud Run runs the container directly, autoscales on request concurrency, scales to zero when idle, and has no cluster to operate.

option_breakdown.A: VMs are billed while they run, don't scale to zero on their own, and mean managing an OS.
option_breakdown.B: GKE means operating a Kubernetes cluster, which the team wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Run functions deploy from source code, not from an existing container image.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Cloud Run runs the container image directly, autoscales on request concurrency, scales to zero when idle, and has no cluster to operate.

questions.title: Small handler with no container pipeline
questions.summary: Cloud Run functions deploy from source with an event trigger and no container tooling.
questions.question: A short Python routine must resize each image as it lands in a Cloud Storage bucket. The team wants to write only the handler function, with no web server code and no Dockerfile, and deploy it from source with a trigger on the bucket. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: Cloud Run functions
options.B: A Cloud Run service
options.C: A GKE Job started for each image
options.D: A Compute Engine VM that polls the bucket

explanation.summary: Cloud Run functions deploy straight from source with an event trigger and no container tooling, which matches a small single-purpose handler.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud Run functions deploy a single handler from source with an event trigger on the bucket and no container tooling.
option_breakdown.B: A service's code must run its own web server listening on the port Cloud Run provides; the team wants to write only the function.
option_breakdown.C: That needs a container image and a cluster to run it, which is far more than a small handler.
option_breakdown.D: A polling VM runs, and is billed, all the time, and the team has to manage its OS.

questions.title: No paying for idle capacity
questions.summary: Scale-to-zero billing means you are charged only while a request is served.
questions.question: A containerised internal tool is used only when an operator opens it, and finance objects to paying for idle capacity between uses. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: A GKE Autopilot cluster running the container.
options.B: A Cloud Run service with minimum instances set to 0.
options.C: An e2-micro VM running the container all month.
options.D: A Cloud Run service with minimum instances set to 1 to avoid cold starts.

explanation.summary: With no minimum instances, Cloud Run scales to zero and charges nothing between uses.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot bills Pod requests while Pods run, and a Deployment keeps its Pods running between uses unless someone scales it to zero by hand.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With no minimum instances, Cloud Run scales to zero and charges nothing between uses.
option_breakdown.C: A VM bills for every hour it runs, used or not.
option_breakdown.D: A minimum instance keeps an instance warm — and billed — between uses, which is exactly what finance objects to.

questions.title: Reuse existing Helm charts
questions.summary: GKE runs the same Kubernetes API, so existing manifests and Helm charts carry over unchanged.
questions.question: A team already runs Kubernetes on-premises with Helm charts and wants to move to the cloud without rewriting their deployment tooling. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: Rewrite each service as a Cloud Run function.
options.B: Package the charts' images and deploy them to Cloud Run services.
options.C: A GKE cluster, deploying the existing charts with helm install.
options.D: Compute Engine VMs running a self-installed Kubernetes distribution.

explanation.summary: GKE is conformant Kubernetes, so the same charts and helm commands work unchanged.

option_breakdown.A: Rewriting everything is exactly what the team wants to avoid, and functions do not consume Helm charts.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Run runs containers but not Kubernetes manifests; Helm charts would have to be translated.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. GKE is conformant Kubernetes, so the same charts and helm commands work unchanged.
option_breakdown.D: Self-managed Kubernetes on VMs would run Helm, but the team would own the control plane, upgrades and availability that GKE manages.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud container clusters get-credentials prod --region=us-central1 && helm install app ./chart

questions.title: Custom machine shape on Spot capacity
questions.summary: Custom machine types and Spot provisioning are Compute Engine features.
questions.question: A cost-sensitive workload must run on Spot capacity with a custom shape of 6 vCPUs and 40 GB of memory, which no predefined machine type provides. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: A sole-tenant node sized for the workload.
options.B: An e2-standard-8 Spot VM, the nearest predefined type above the requirement.
options.C: Cloud Run with 6 vCPUs and 40 GiB of memory per instance.
options.D: An N2 custom machine type with 6 vCPUs and 40 GB, as a Spot VM.

explanation.summary: Custom machine types set vCPU and memory independently, and Spot is a provisioning model on the same VM — the two combine on Compute Engine.

option_breakdown.A: Sole tenancy is for physical isolation and licensing; it is the most expensive option, not a Spot discount.
option_breakdown.B: e2-standard-8 has 8 vCPUs and 32 GB: it wastes CPU and still lacks memory.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Run caps an instance well below 40 GiB and has no Spot provisioning model.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Custom machine types set vCPU and memory independently, and Spot is a provisioning model on the same VM — the two combine on Compute Engine.

questions.title: Nightly two-hour batch at lowest cost
questions.summary: Interruption-tolerant batch on Spot VMs is the cheapest compute on Google Cloud.
questions.question: A set of batch processing jobs runs nightly, takes about two hours, and tolerates interruption because it checkpoints and restarts. You want to minimise cost. What should you choose?

options.A: Spot VMs in a managed instance group.
options.B: On-demand VMs covered by a three-year committed use discount.
options.C: A GKE Standard cluster with on-demand nodes that run all day.
options.D: Cloud Run functions, one invocation per batch job.

explanation.summary: Interruption-tolerant, restartable work is the Spot case: a large discount, and preemption costs only the time since the last checkpoint. The MIG recreates preempted VMs.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Interruption-tolerant, restartable work is the Spot case: a large discount, and preemption costs only the time since the last checkpoint. The MIG recreates preempted VMs.
option_breakdown.B: A commitment bills 24 hours a day for three years to run two hours a night.
option_breakdown.C: Always-on on-demand nodes pay for 22 idle hours and forgo the Spot discount.
option_breakdown.D: A two-hour job exceeds what a single function invocation is designed for, and it is not the cheapest compute for sustained batch.

questions.title: Lift-and-shift MySQL, one region
questions.summary: Cloud SQL is drop-in managed MySQL covering this size and throughput with no application change.
questions.question: An existing MySQL application must move to Google Cloud with no schema changes. It peaks at 400 GB and a few hundred transactions per second, all in one region. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Spanner
options.B: Cloud SQL
options.C: BigQuery
options.D: Firestore

explanation.summary: Cloud SQL is a drop-in managed MySQL that comfortably covers this size and throughput with automated backups, replicas and patching, and requires no application change.

option_breakdown.A: Spanner has no MySQL engine; moving to it means schema and driver changes, for scale this workload doesn't need.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud SQL for MySQL is a drop-in managed MySQL that covers this size and throughput, with automated backups, replicas and patching, and no application change.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not a transactional MySQL back end.
option_breakdown.D: Firestore is a document database; the relational schema would have to be redesigned.

questions.title: Globally consistent payments ledger
questions.summary: Spanner alone combines relational semantics, external consistency and multi-region synchronous replication.
questions.question: A relational payments ledger, queried with SQL, must provide strongly consistent transactions across three continents with a 99.999% availability target. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Firestore
options.B: Bigtable
options.C: Spanner
options.D: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

explanation.summary: Spanner is the only Google Cloud database that combines relational semantics, external consistency and multi-region synchronous replication at a five-nines SLA.

option_breakdown.A: Firestore is a document database, not relational, and its multi-region locations stay within one continent.
option_breakdown.B: Bigtable has no SQL transactions, and replication between its clusters is eventually consistent.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Spanner combines relational semantics, external consistency and synchronous multi-region replication with a 99.999% SLA.
option_breakdown.D: AlloyDB is regional; its cross-region replicas are asynchronous copies for disaster recovery.

questions.title: Ad-hoc SQL over 900 TB of clickstream
questions.summary: BigQuery separates storage from compute and scans petabytes with no provisioned servers.
questions.question: Analysts must run ad-hoc SQL over eight years of clickstream data totalling 900 TB, with no infrastructure to manage and cost charged per query. Which product should you choose?

options.A: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
options.B: Memorystore
options.C: Cloud SQL
options.D: BigQuery

explanation.summary: BigQuery separates storage from compute and scans petabytes without provisioned servers, which is precisely the serverless analytics case.

option_breakdown.A: AlloyDB is a provisioned PostgreSQL database billed per instance; 900 TB of ad-hoc scans is not its case.
option_breakdown.B: Memorystore is an in-memory cache, not an analytics engine for 900 TB.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud SQL storage tops out far below 900 TB, and it is billed per instance, not per query.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. BigQuery separates storage from compute and scans petabytes without provisioned servers, with on-demand pricing per query.

explanation.gcloud_command: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM `p.ds.clicks` GROUP BY country'

questions.title: Two million sensor writes per second
questions.summary: Bigtable is built for very high sustained writes and low-latency lookups on a composite row key.
questions.question: An IoT platform ingests two million sensor readings per second and reads them back by device ID and time range with single-digit millisecond latency. No joins or multi-row transactions are needed, and cost matters. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Bigtable
options.B: Cloud SQL
options.C: Spanner
options.D: BigQuery

explanation.summary: Bigtable is built for exactly this: extremely high sustained write throughput and low-latency lookups on a row key that encodes device and timestamp.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Bigtable is built for this: very high sustained write throughput and low-latency range reads on a row key that encodes device and timestamp.
option_breakdown.B: A Cloud SQL instance has one primary for writes, which cannot absorb two million writes per second.
option_breakdown.C: Spanner could scale this far, but you'd pay for relational features and transactions the workload doesn't use.
option_breakdown.D: BigQuery is built for analytical scans, not single-digit millisecond reads of one device's rows.

questions.title: Mobile app that works offline
questions.summary: Firestore's client SDKs provide real-time listeners and offline persistence natively.
questions.question: A collaborative mobile application needs documents that synchronise to clients in real time and keep working while the device is offline, resynchronising when connectivity returns. Which product should you choose?

options.A: BigQuery
options.B: Firestore
options.C: Bigtable
options.D: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

explanation.summary: Firestore's client SDKs provide real-time listeners and offline persistence with automatic re-sync, which no other Google Cloud database offers natively.

option_breakdown.A: BigQuery is an analytics warehouse with no client sync or offline mode.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Firestore's client SDKs provide real-time listeners and offline persistence with automatic resynchronisation.
option_breakdown.C: Bigtable has no mobile SDKs and no offline sync; you'd build both yourself.
option_breakdown.D: AlloyDB is a server-side database; the app would need its own sync layer to work offline.

questions.title: Cache computed sessions sub-millisecond
questions.summary: Memorystore provides managed Redis with sub-millisecond in-memory reads as a cache tier.
questions.question: A read-heavy API must cut database load by caching computed session objects, with sub-millisecond reads. The data can be rebuilt if lost. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Bigtable
options.B: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
options.C: Memorystore
options.D: Cloud SQL

explanation.summary: Memorystore provides managed Redis with sub-millisecond in-memory reads, which is the standard cache tier in front of a primary database.

option_breakdown.A: Bigtable is a durable store with millisecond latency, not a sub-millisecond in-memory cache.
option_breakdown.B: Another database doesn't reduce load on the first one, and it isn't an in-memory cache.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Memorystore provides managed Redis or Valkey with sub-millisecond in-memory reads, the standard cache in front of a primary database.
option_breakdown.D: Adding a Cloud SQL instance adds a database; it doesn't give sub-millisecond cached reads.

questions.title: PostgreSQL with heavy analytical queries
questions.summary: AlloyDB adds a columnar engine on top of PostgreSQL compatibility for mixed workloads.
questions.question: A PostgreSQL workload runs heavy analytical queries alongside its transactional load, and latency has become unacceptable on Cloud SQL. The team wants to stay PostgreSQL-compatible. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Cloud SQL
options.B: Spanner
options.C: BigQuery
options.D: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

explanation.summary: AlloyDB adds a columnar engine and machine-learning-driven caching on top of PostgreSQL compatibility, targeting exactly this mixed transactional and analytical profile.

option_breakdown.A: The workload is already too slow on Cloud SQL; a larger instance of the same engine adds no columnar analytics.
option_breakdown.B: Spanner has a PostgreSQL interface but is a different engine; it means a migration and is not aimed at analytics on live transactional data.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery could take the analytics, but it can't serve the PostgreSQL transactional load, so the app would be split in two.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. AlloyDB adds a columnar engine and adaptive caching to PostgreSQL compatibility, aimed at this mixed transactional and analytical profile.

questions.title: Outgrown the largest Cloud SQL machine
questions.summary: Spanner scales writes horizontally while preserving relational semantics, removing app-level sharding.
questions.question: A relational workload has outgrown the largest available Cloud SQL machine type and must keep scaling writes, without the team implementing sharding in the application. Which product should you choose?

options.A: Spanner, adding compute capacity as writes grow.
options.B: A Cloud SQL read replica in each zone.
options.C: Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus with high availability.
options.D: Memorystore for Redis in front of Cloud SQL.

explanation.summary: Spanner scales writes horizontally while keeping relational semantics and strong consistency, so the application needs no sharding.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Spanner scales writes horizontally while keeping relational semantics and strong consistency, so the application needs no sharding.
option_breakdown.B: Read replicas scale reads only; every write still goes to the single primary.
option_breakdown.C: Enterprise Plus is faster and more available, but it is still one primary with a single machine's write ceiling.
option_breakdown.D: A cache absorbs reads, not writes.

questions.title: Images served to a public website
questions.summary: With frequent reads, Standard's lack of retrieval fees makes it cheapest overall.
questions.question: A bucket serves the images for a public website and every object is read many times a day. Which storage class minimises total cost?

options.A: Nearline Storage
options.B: Standard Storage
options.C: Coldline Storage
options.D: Archive Storage

explanation.summary: Standard is the only class without a retrieval fee or minimum duration, so for frequently read data it is also the cheapest overall despite the higher storage price.

option_breakdown.A: Nearline charges a retrieval fee on every read, and many reads a day make that the largest cost.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Standard has no retrieval fee or minimum duration, so for data read many times a day it is the cheapest overall despite the higher storage price.
option_breakdown.C: Coldline's retrieval fees are higher still, and it is designed for data read about once a quarter.
option_breakdown.D: Archive has the highest retrieval fees of all, so frequent reads make it the most expensive.

questions.title: Monthly reporting extracts kept two years
questions.summary: A once-a-month read pattern fits Nearline's 30-day minimum and per-read fee.
questions.question: A new reporting extract is written to Cloud Storage each month. Analysts open every extract about once a month for the two years it is kept, and no extract is deleted early. Which storage class does Google recommend for this access pattern?

options.A: Archive Storage
options.B: Standard Storage
options.C: Nearline Storage
options.D: Coldline Storage

explanation.summary: Google's guidance places data read or modified about once a month in Nearline, which has a 30-day minimum storage duration and a per-GB retrieval fee.

option_breakdown.A: Archive is for data read less than once a year; monthly reads would pay its highest retrieval fee twelve times a year.
option_breakdown.B: Standard is for frequently accessed, hot data; monthly access is the Nearline case.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Nearline is the recommended class for data accessed about once a month, and two years far exceeds its 30-day minimum.
option_breakdown.D: Coldline is for data accessed at most once a quarter; monthly reads make its higher retrieval fee add up.

questions.title: Quarterly audit evidence, instant retrieval
questions.summary: Coldline's 90-day minimum matches quarterly access and still returns objects immediately.
questions.question: Audit evidence is kept in Cloud Storage for five years and realistically opened about four times a year. When it is opened, it must be readable immediately. Which storage class minimises total cost?

options.A: Nearline Storage
options.B: Archive Storage
options.C: Standard Storage
options.D: Coldline Storage

explanation.summary: All storage classes return data in milliseconds. For data read about once a quarter, Coldline's lower storage price outweighs its retrieval fees.

option_breakdown.A: Nearline's storage price is higher than Coldline's, and quarterly reads don't need its lower retrieval fee.
option_breakdown.B: Archive is also readable immediately, but its retrieval fee is the highest, so four full reads a year cost more than Coldline.
option_breakdown.C: Standard has no retrieval fee, but its storage price is the highest, which dominates for rarely read data.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Coldline is designed for data accessed about once a quarter, and every class, Coldline included, returns objects in milliseconds.

questions.title: Seven years of regulatory records
questions.summary: For data that may never be read, Archive's storage price dominates total cost.
questions.question: Seven years of regulatory records must be retained at the lowest possible storage cost. They will be read only if a regulator asks, which may never happen. Which class should you choose?

options.A: Archive Storage
options.B: Standard Storage
options.C: Nearline Storage
options.D: Coldline Storage

explanation.summary: For data that may never be read, Archive's lowest storage price dominates the total cost even though its retrieval fee is the highest.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. For data that may never be read, Archive's lowest storage price dominates the total cost, even though its retrieval fee is the highest.
option_breakdown.B: Standard has the highest storage price, paid every month for seven years on data nobody reads.
option_breakdown.C: Nearline costs more to store than Archive, and its lower retrieval fee is worth nothing if the data is never read.
option_breakdown.D: Coldline is cheaper than Nearline but still costs more to store than Archive.

questions.title: Nightly backups restored monthly
questions.summary: Monthly restores and 90-day retention fit Nearline's minimum duration exactly.
questions.question: Backup images are written to Cloud Storage nightly and deleted after 60 days. About once a month, a recovery drill restores one backup. Which bucket setup minimises cost without incurring early-deletion charges?

options.A: Coldline default class, with a lifecycle rule deleting objects at 60 days.
options.B: Nearline default class, with a lifecycle rule deleting objects at 60 days.
options.C: Standard default class, moving objects to Archive after 30 days.
options.D: Standard default class, with a lifecycle rule deleting objects at 60 days.

explanation.summary: Nearline's 30-day minimum is met by a 60-day life, and its storage price is half of Standard's. Coldline and Archive would be deleted before their minimum durations.

option_breakdown.A: Deleting at 60 days is before Coldline's 90-day minimum, so early-deletion charges apply.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Sixty days is well past Nearline's 30-day minimum, and occasional restores keep its retrieval fees small.
option_breakdown.C: Archive has a 365-day minimum, so deleting at 60 days incurs early-deletion charges.
option_breakdown.D: Standard has no minimum, but it stores rarely read backups at twice Nearline's price.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage buckets create gs://backups --location=us-central1 --default-storage-class=NEARLINE
gcloud storage buckets update gs://backups --lifecycle-file=delete-60d.json

questions.title: Path routing with managed TLS worldwide
questions.summary: Path routing, managed TLS and a global anycast IP are properties of the global external ALB.
questions.question: A public website must route /api to one backend and /static to another, terminate TLS with a Google-managed certificate, and serve users worldwide from the nearest edge. Which load balancer should you deploy?

options.A: External passthrough Network Load Balancer
options.B: Regional internal Application Load Balancer
options.C: Global external Application Load Balancer
options.D: Regional external Application Load Balancer

explanation.summary: Path-based routing, managed TLS termination and a single global anycast IP are all properties of the global external Application Load Balancer.

option_breakdown.A: It is a layer 4 passthrough: no URL paths, no TLS termination, and no global edge.
option_breakdown.B: It serves clients inside the VPC only, not a public website.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Path-based routing, managed TLS termination and one global anycast IP served from Google's edge are all features of the global external Application Load Balancer.
option_breakdown.D: It routes paths and terminates TLS, but from one region, not from the edge nearest each user.

questions.title: UDP game server preserving client IP
questions.summary: Passthrough load balancing forwards packets unproxied, supporting UDP and preserving source IP.
questions.question: A game server exposes a UDP protocol to the internet, and the backend must observe the original client source IP address. Which load balancer should you deploy?

options.A: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer
options.B: External proxy Network Load Balancer
options.C: Global external Application Load Balancer
options.D: External passthrough Network Load Balancer

explanation.summary: Passthrough load balancing forwards packets without proxying, which both supports arbitrary UDP and leaves the client source IP intact.

option_breakdown.A: It is internal only, so it cannot receive traffic from the internet.
option_breakdown.B: The proxy load balancer handles TCP, not UDP, and backends see the proxy's address.
option_breakdown.C: It carries HTTP and HTTPS only, not a UDP game protocol.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A passthrough load balancer forwards packets without proxying, so it carries UDP and leaves the client source IP intact.

questions.title: Internal HTTPS with host-based routing
questions.summary: The internal ALB provides layer 7 routing on a private VPC address.
questions.question: A microservice must be reachable over HTTPS only by other services inside the VPC, with host-based routing between two versions. Which load balancer should you deploy?

options.A: Regional internal Application Load Balancer
options.B: Global external Application Load Balancer
options.C: External passthrough Network Load Balancer
options.D: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer

explanation.summary: The internal Application Load Balancer provides layer 7 routing on a private VPC address, which keeps the service off the internet while still supporting host rules.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The internal Application Load Balancer provides layer 7 routing on a private VPC address, keeping the service off the internet while supporting host rules.
option_breakdown.B: It is internet-facing, which the service must not be.
option_breakdown.C: It is internet-facing and works at layer 4, with no host-based routing.
option_breakdown.D: It is internal but works at layer 4, so it can't route on the HTTP host.

questions.title: Insert third-party firewall appliances
questions.summary: The internal passthrough NLB is the supported next hop for appliance insertion.
questions.question: Traffic from several subnets must be distributed across a pool of third-party firewall appliances, which must receive unmodified packets. Which load balancer should you deploy?

options.A: Regional internal Application Load Balancer
options.B: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer
options.C: External proxy Network Load Balancer
options.D: Global external Application Load Balancer

explanation.summary: The internal passthrough Network Load Balancer is the supported next-hop for appliance insertion because it forwards packets without rewriting them.

option_breakdown.A: It terminates HTTP and opens new connections to backends, so the appliances wouldn't see the original packets.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The internal passthrough Network Load Balancer can be a route's next hop, and it forwards packets without rewriting them.
option_breakdown.C: It is an internet-facing TCP proxy, not a next hop for traffic between subnets.
option_breakdown.D: It is an internet-facing HTTP proxy, not a next hop inside the VPC.

questions.title: TLS offload for a non-HTTP TCP service
questions.summary: The external proxy NLB terminates TLS at the edge for arbitrary TCP protocols.
questions.question: A public TCP service on port 9000 needs TLS offloaded at Google's edge, but it does not speak HTTP. Which load balancer should you deploy?

options.A: Global external Application Load Balancer
options.B: External passthrough Network Load Balancer
options.C: External proxy Network Load Balancer
options.D: Regional internal Application Load Balancer

explanation.summary: The external proxy Network Load Balancer terminates TLS at the edge for arbitrary TCP protocols, which is the case HTTP-based load balancers cannot cover.

option_breakdown.A: It handles HTTP and HTTPS only, and the service doesn't speak HTTP.
option_breakdown.B: A passthrough load balancer doesn't terminate TLS; the backends would have to.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The external proxy Network Load Balancer terminates TLS at Google's edge for any TCP protocol.
option_breakdown.D: It is internal, and it handles HTTP only.

questions.title: Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor in front of an app
questions.summary: Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor attach to the external ALB's backend services and edge.
questions.question: The team wants Cloud CDN caching and Cloud Armor security policies applied in front of a containerised web application. Which load balancer is a prerequisite?

options.A: A LoadBalancer Service with an external passthrough Network Load Balancer.
options.B: An internal Application Load Balancer.
options.C: Cloud Armor attached to the VPC firewall.
options.D: A global external Application Load Balancer.

explanation.summary: Both Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor are enabled on the backend service of an external Application Load Balancer, which is therefore the prerequisite.

option_breakdown.A: A passthrough layer 4 load balancer has no HTTP backend service to cache from or protect.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud CDN is for internet-facing external Application Load Balancers; an internal one serves only private clients.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Armor policies attach to load balancer backend services, not to VPC firewall rules.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Both Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor are enabled on the backend service of an external Application Load Balancer, which is therefore the prerequisite.

questions.title: Central network team, many app projects
questions.summary: Shared VPC separates network ownership (host project) from workload ownership (service projects).
questions.question: Brightwater Insurance has twelve application teams, each with its own project. The central network team must keep exclusive control of subnets, routes and firewall rules, while the application teams deploy VMs into those subnets. What should you set up?

options.A: Set up Shared VPC: one host project, with the app projects as service projects.
options.B: Connect each team's VPC to a central VPC with VPC Network Peering.
options.C: Give each team its own custom-mode VPC in its own project.
options.D: Grant the network team Compute Network Admin in each of the twelve projects.

explanation.summary: Shared VPC is designed for exactly this separation: the host project owns the network objects while service projects deploy resources into subnets they cannot modify.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Shared VPC separates the roles: the host project owns subnets, routes and firewall rules, while service projects deploy into subnets they can't modify.
option_breakdown.B: Each team would still own, and could change, its own VPC.
option_breakdown.C: Each team would control its own subnets and firewall rules, the opposite of what's required.
option_breakdown.D: The network team gets rights, but project owners keep theirs, so control is not exclusive.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute shared-vpc enable HOST_PROJECT
gcloud compute shared-vpc associated-projects add SERVICE_PROJECT --host-project=HOST_PROJECT

questions.title: Private traffic between two organisations
questions.summary: VPC Peering connects networks across organisations over Google's backbone with no gateway.
questions.question: Two VPC networks in different organisations, with non-overlapping ranges, must exchange private traffic at low latency without leaving Google's network, and with no gateways or tunnels to manage. What should you do?

options.A: Set up Cloud Interconnect between the two organisations.
options.B: Configure VPC Network Peering between the networks.
options.C: Create HA VPN tunnels between the networks.
options.D: Configure Shared VPC with one network as the host.

explanation.summary: VPC Network Peering connects networks across organisations over Google's backbone with private RFC 1918 reachability and no gateway to manage.

option_breakdown.A: Interconnect connects on-premises networks to Google Cloud, not two VPCs to each other.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. VPC Network Peering connects networks across organisations over Google's network, with private reachability and no gateway to manage.
option_breakdown.C: HA VPN works, but it means gateways and tunnels to manage, with per-tunnel bandwidth limits.
option_breakdown.D: Shared VPC works only within one organisation.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings create to-partner --network=prod-vpc \
  --peer-project=PARTNER_PROJECT --peer-network=partner-vpc

questions.title: Address plan must match on-premises
questions.summary: Custom-mode VPCs let you choose every subnet range and region deliberately.
questions.question: The address plan must align with an existing on-premises IP scheme to avoid overlap, and subnets should exist only in the two regions actually in use. What should you do?

options.A: Create an auto-mode VPC and delete the subnets in unused regions.
options.B: Configure VPC Network Peering with the on-premises network.
options.C: Create a custom-mode VPC and define the subnets explicitly.
options.D: Create an auto-mode VPC.

explanation.summary: Custom-mode VPCs let you choose every subnet range and region deliberately, which is what avoiding overlap with on-premises addressing requires.

option_breakdown.A: Auto-mode subnets use fixed ranges from 10.128.0.0/9, which may still overlap on-premises.
option_breakdown.B: Peering connects two VPC networks; it doesn't reach on-premises or choose address ranges.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A custom-mode VPC lets you pick every subnet range and region, which is what avoiding overlap with on-premises addressing requires.
option_breakdown.D: Auto mode creates a subnet in every region from predefined ranges, not just two regions in your own scheme.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks create prod-vpc --subnet-mode=custom
gcloud compute networks subnets create app-us --network=prod-vpc \
  --region=us-central1 --range=10.20.0.0/20

questions.title: Peering is not transitive
questions.summary: Peering is explicitly non-transitive; C must peer directly with A.
questions.question: Network A is already peered with network B. Network C must now also reach A, and a colleague suggests routing the traffic through B. What should you do?

options.A: Enable custom route export on the A–B peering so C's traffic can pass through B.
options.B: Make B a Shared VPC host with A and C as service projects.
options.C: Add static routes in C whose next hop is a VM in B.
options.D: Create a new peering directly between C and A.

explanation.summary: Peering is non-transitive, so C must peer directly with A (both sides create the peering).

option_breakdown.A: Peering is non-transitive: exporting routes does not let traffic transit B to a third network.
option_breakdown.B: Converting existing networks into a Shared VPC is a redesign, and A and C already have their own networks.
option_breakdown.C: A static route's next-hop instance must be in the route's own VPC, so C cannot route through a VM in B — and an appliance hop would be an assembled workaround anyway.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Peering is non-transitive, so C must peer directly with A (both sides create the peering).

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings create c-to-a --network=vpc-c \
  --peer-network=vpc-a --peer-project=PROJECT_A

questions.title: Cross-project private communication without a mesh
questions.summary: Service projects share the host network directly, so no peering mesh is needed.
questions.question: Internal microservices spread across several projects must communicate over private addresses, and the platform team refuses to maintain a growing mesh of peerings. What should you do?

options.A: Make one project the Shared VPC host and attach the other projects as service projects.
options.B: Peer every project's VPC with every other project's VPC.
options.C: Connect the projects' VPCs with HA VPN tunnels.
options.D: Give each service an external IP and restrict access with firewall rules.

explanation.summary: With Shared VPC, workloads in every service project use subnets of one network, so they talk over private addresses with no peerings at all.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. With Shared VPC, workloads in every service project use subnets of one network, so they talk over private addresses with no peerings at all.
option_breakdown.B: A full mesh of peerings is exactly what the platform team refuses to maintain, and peering is non-transitive.
option_breakdown.C: VPN tunnels between VPCs add gateways, cost and bandwidth limits to what should be one network.
option_breakdown.D: External IPs put internal traffic on public addresses, which violates the private-address requirement.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute shared-vpc associated-projects add SERVICE_PROJECT --host-project=HOST_PROJECT

questions.title: Tier-to-tier rule in a shared subnet
questions.subtopic: Secure Tags and Service Accounts in Rules
questions.summary: Scoping by service account or tag expresses tier-to-tier intent independently of IP addressing.
questions.question: Only the web tier may receive traffic on port 8080 from the application tier. The two tiers share a subnet, so a CIDR-based rule would be far too broad. What should you configure?

options.A: An ingress rule allowing tcp:8080 from the subnet's range to all instances.
options.B: An ingress rule allowing tcp:8080 from the app tier's service account to the web tier's.
options.C: An ingress rule allowing tcp:8080 from the app tier's tag, with no target set.
options.D: An egress rule allowing tcp:8080 from the app tier to the web tier.

explanation.summary: Scoping the rule by target and source service account (or network tag) expresses tier-to-tier intent independently of IP addressing, which is what a shared subnet requires.

option_breakdown.A: The subnet holds both tiers and anything else in it, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Scoping the rule by source and target service account expresses tier-to-tier intent independently of IP addresses, which a shared subnet needs.
option_breakdown.C: A rule with no target applies to every instance in the network, not only the web tier.
option_breakdown.D: Egress is already allowed by default; what's missing is an ingress rule on the web tier.

questions.title: All backends unhealthy behind a new LB
questions.summary: Health check probes come from Google's dedicated ranges and must be explicitly allowed.
questions.question: Delmar Outfitters put its catalogue VMs behind a new external Application Load Balancer, and every backend shows as unhealthy. The application answers correctly when you curl it from another VM in the same VPC, and the VPC has only the rules the team created for internal traffic. What should you configure?

options.A: Assign external IP addresses to the backend VMs.
options.B: Allow ingress from 35.235.240.0/20, the IAP TCP forwarding range.
options.C: Allow ingress from Google's health check ranges, 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22.
options.D: Allow egress from the backends to 0.0.0.0/0.

explanation.summary: Health check probes originate from Google's dedicated ranges; if those are not explicitly allowed to reach the backends, every instance fails its check regardless of application health.

option_breakdown.A: The load balancer reaches backends on their internal addresses; external IPs aren't needed.
option_breakdown.B: That range carries IAP TCP forwarding, such as SSH, not health check probes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Health check probes come from Google's dedicated ranges; unless an ingress rule allows them, every backend fails its check whatever the application's state.
option_breakdown.D: Egress is allowed by default, and probes are inbound connections.

questions.title: SSH to VMs with no external IP
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH through Google's frontend from a fixed source range.
questions.question: Administrators must SSH to VMs that have no external IP address, and the team does not want to deploy and maintain a bastion host. Which firewall rule do you need, following least privilege?

options.A: Allow ingress on tcp:22 from 0.0.0.0/0.
options.B: Allow ingress on tcp:22 from 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22.
options.C: Allow egress on tcp:22 to 35.235.240.0/20.
options.D: Allow ingress on tcp:22 from 35.235.240.0/20.

explanation.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH through Google's frontend, so the instances need only accept connections from the IAP range and never require a public address.

option_breakdown.A: It would admit IAP's connections, but it also opens SSH to every source that can route to the VMs.
option_breakdown.B: Those are the health check ranges; IAP connections don't come from them.
option_breakdown.C: IAP connections arrive as inbound traffic, so an egress rule doesn't admit them.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH through Google, so the VMs only need to accept port 22 from the IAP range and never need a public address.

questions.title: Restrict outbound to an approved mirror
questions.summary: The implied egress allow is priority 65535, so a lower-numbered deny plus a narrow allow yields default-deny.
questions.question: VMs reach the internet through Cloud NAT. If a workload is compromised, it must not be able to reach arbitrary internet destinations; only an approved package mirror is permitted. Which firewall configuration should you create?

options.A: An egress deny-all rule at priority 65000, plus an egress allow rule for the mirror at priority 1000.
options.B: An ingress deny rule for 0.0.0.0/0 at priority 1000.
options.C: Delete the implied allow-egress rule, then add an egress allow rule for the mirror.
options.D: An egress allow rule for the mirror at priority 1000.

explanation.summary: Every VPC has an implied allow-egress rule at the lowest priority (65535). A deny-all egress rule at a higher priority overrides it, and an allow for the mirror at a higher priority still lets that one destination through.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The deny at 65000 overrides the implied allow, and the mirror's allow at 1000 is evaluated first.
option_breakdown.B: Ingress rules control inbound traffic; outbound connections stay allowed.
option_breakdown.C: Implied rules can't be deleted; they can only be overridden by rules with a higher priority.
option_breakdown.D: Without a deny rule, the implied allow-egress rule still lets every destination through.

questions.title: RDP to the internet must be impossible
questions.summary: Hierarchical policies evaluate before VPC rules and cannot be overridden at project level.
questions.question: Security must guarantee that no project anywhere in the organisation can open RDP to the internet, and project owners must not be able to override the control. What should you configure?

options.A: A VPC firewall rule in every project denying tcp:3389 from 0.0.0.0/0 at priority 0.
options.B: A hierarchical firewall policy on the organisation denying tcp:3389 from 0.0.0.0/0.
options.C: An IAM deny policy that blocks compute.firewalls.create for everyone.
options.D: A Security Command Center notification for open RDP findings.

explanation.summary: Rules in a hierarchical firewall policy on the organisation are evaluated before VPC firewall rules, and project owners can't change them, so a deny there can't be overridden.

option_breakdown.A: Project owners can delete or override their own VPC rules, and new projects lack the rule.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A deny rule in an organisation-level hierarchical policy is evaluated first and is out of reach of project owners.
option_breakdown.C: It stops every firewall change, including legitimate ones, and doesn't touch rules that already exist.
option_breakdown.D: A finding reports open RDP after it exists; it prevents nothing.

questions.title: Rules that survive autoscaling
questions.subtopic: Secure Tags and Service Accounts in Rules
questions.summary: Tags and service accounts follow the instance template, so rules survive instance replacement.
questions.question: A database tier must accept connections only from the application tier, and the rule must keep working as the autoscaler destroys and recreates instances with new IP addresses. What should you configure?

options.A: Allow ingress on the database port from the application tier's current internal IP addresses.
options.B: Allow ingress on the database port from the whole subnet range.
options.C: Allow ingress from the app tier's service account to the database tier's service account.
options.D: Allow ingress on the database port from 0.0.0.0/0, relying on the absence of external IPs.

explanation.summary: Service accounts come from the instance template, so the rule follows every new instance with no IP in it — and changing an instance's service account requires stopping it.

option_breakdown.A: Autoscaled instances get new IP addresses, so an IP list breaks at the next scale event.
option_breakdown.B: The subnet may hold other workloads, which would also reach the database.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Service accounts come from the instance template, so the rule follows every new instance with no IP in it — and changing an instance's service account requires stopping it.
option_breakdown.D: An open source range lets anything that can route to the database connect.

questions.title: Kubernetes without managing nodes
questions.summary: Autopilot is fully managed GKE: Google runs the nodes and bills per Pod request.
questions.question: A small team wants Kubernetes on GKE without sizing, patching or scaling nodes, and wants to pay for the resources their Pods request rather than for nodes. How should you create the GKE cluster?

options.A: Create a regional standard cluster with nodes across three zones.
options.B: Create a zonal standard cluster.
options.C: Create a private cluster with no public endpoint and authorised networks for control plane access.
options.D: Create a GKE Autopilot cluster.

explanation.summary: Autopilot is the fully managed GKE mode: Google manages the nodes entirely and billing is per Pod resource request rather than per node.

option_breakdown.A: A regional Standard cluster still has node pools to size and upgrade, and you pay per node.
option_breakdown.B: A zonal Standard cluster has the same node management and per-node billing.
option_breakdown.C: Private networking changes exposure, not who manages the nodes.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Autopilot is the fully managed GKE mode: Google manages the nodes, and billing is based on Pod resource requests.

questions.title: Control plane must survive a zone loss
questions.summary: Only a regional cluster replicates the control plane across three zones.
questions.question: A team runs GKE Standard because its workloads need node-level customisation. The GKE cluster's control plane and its workloads must survive the loss of a single zone, so that deployments can continue during a zonal outage. How should you create the cluster?

options.A: As a regional Standard cluster, with nodes in three zones.
options.B: As a zonal Standard cluster, with node locations in three zones.
options.C: As a zonal Standard cluster with private nodes.
options.D: As a zonal Standard cluster with node auto-repair enabled.

explanation.summary: Only a regional cluster replicates the control plane across zones. A multi-zonal cluster spreads nodes, but its control plane is still in one zone.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A regional cluster runs control plane replicas and nodes in several zones, so the API server and workloads survive a zone loss.
option_breakdown.B: The nodes survive, but the control plane stays in one zone, so deployments stop if that zone fails.
option_breakdown.C: Private nodes change exposure, not availability.
option_breakdown.D: Auto-repair replaces unhealthy nodes in the same zone; it doesn't help when the zone is down.

questions.title: No public IPs on nodes
questions.summary: Private nodes plus authorised networks removes public addressing and restricts the endpoint.
questions.question: Compliance forbids GKE nodes from having public IP addresses, and the GKE control plane must be reachable only from the corporate network. How should you create the GKE cluster?

options.A: As an Autopilot cluster with default networking.
options.B: With private nodes, and authorised networks limited to the corporate ranges.
options.C: As a regional Standard cluster with nodes across three zones.
options.D: As a zonal Standard cluster.

explanation.summary: A private cluster gives nodes internal addresses only, and authorised networks restricts which source ranges may reach the control plane endpoint.

option_breakdown.A: With default networking, the control plane endpoint is reachable from any address; Autopilot changes who manages nodes, not exposure.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Private nodes have internal addresses only, and authorised networks restrict which source ranges can reach the control plane.
option_breakdown.C: A regional cluster improves availability; its nodes and endpoint can still be public.
option_breakdown.D: A zonal cluster says nothing about node addresses or control plane access.

questions.title: Dedicated nodes for one workload
questions.summary: A tainted GPU node pool confines expensive hardware to workloads that tolerate the taint.
questions.question: In an existing GKE Standard cluster, an in-memory analytics workload needs memory-optimised M3 nodes. All other Pods must stay on the cheaper general-purpose nodes and must never be scheduled onto the M3 nodes. What should you do?

options.A: Change the default node pool's machine type to M3.
options.B: Add an M3 node pool, label its nodes, and add a nodeSelector to the analytics Pods.
options.C: Add an M3 node pool with a taint, and a matching toleration on the analytics Pods.
options.D: Enable node auto-provisioning on the cluster with M3 limits.

explanation.summary: A taint repels every Pod that doesn't tolerate it, so a tainted M3 node pool keeps other Pods off it while the analytics Pods tolerate the taint.

option_breakdown.A: Every Pod would then run on M3 nodes, which is what must not happen.
option_breakdown.B: A nodeSelector attracts the analytics Pods but doesn't keep other Pods off the M3 nodes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Only Pods that tolerate the taint can run on the M3 pool, and the analytics Pods tolerate it.
option_breakdown.D: Auto-provisioning creates node pools on demand; by itself it doesn't keep other Pods off the M3 nodes it creates.

questions.title: Security defaults that cannot be disabled
questions.summary: Autopilot enables and enforces these defaults as part of the managed mode.
questions.question: Management wants GKE's hardening defaults — Workload Identity, Shielded nodes and node auto-upgrade — enforced without the team being able to turn them off. How should you configure the cluster?

options.A: A GKE Standard cluster with those features enabled at creation.
options.B: A GKE Standard cluster with an organisation policy on the node pool machine type.
options.C: A GKE Standard cluster on the Stable release channel.
options.D: A GKE Autopilot cluster.

explanation.summary: Autopilot enables these hardening defaults as part of the mode and does not let you turn them off.

option_breakdown.A: On Standard the features can be enabled, but the team can also disable them later.
option_breakdown.B: A machine-type restriction does not enforce Workload Identity, Shielded nodes or auto-upgrade.
option_breakdown.C: A release channel controls the pace of upgrades; it enforces none of the other defaults.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Autopilot enables these hardening defaults as part of the mode and does not let you turn them off.

questions.title: Zero-RPO failover for one database VM
questions.summary: Regional PD replicates writes synchronously to a second zone and can be force-attached there.
questions.question: A single-instance database must be able to fail over to another zone with its data intact and a recovery point objective of zero. Which storage should you attach?

options.A: A regional Persistent Disk
options.B: A zonal Persistent Disk
options.C: A zonal Persistent Disk with a snapshot schedule every hour
options.D: Local SSD

explanation.summary: Regional Persistent Disk replicates writes synchronously to a second zone, so the disk can be force-attached to a replacement instance there with no data loss.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Regional Persistent Disk replicates writes synchronously to a second zone, so the disk can be force-attached to a replacement instance there with no data loss.
option_breakdown.B: A zonal disk lives in one zone; if the zone is lost, the data is unavailable there.
option_breakdown.C: Hourly snapshots can lose up to an hour of writes, so the recovery point is not zero.
option_breakdown.D: Local SSD is lost when the VM stops, and it can't move to another zone.

questions.title: Scratch space rebuilt every run
questions.summary: Local SSD offers the lowest latency and highest IOPS; its ephemerality is acceptable here.
questions.question: A data-processing job needs the highest possible IOPS for scratch space that is rebuilt from Cloud Storage at the start of every run. Which storage should you attach?

options.A: Google Cloud Hyperdisk
options.B: Local SSD
options.C: Filestore
options.D: A zonal Persistent Disk

explanation.summary: Local SSD offers the lowest latency and highest IOPS available, and its ephemerality is acceptable precisely because the data is regenerated each run.

option_breakdown.A: Hyperdisk is network-attached; it is fast, but Local SSD has lower latency and higher IOPS.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Local SSD gives the lowest latency and highest IOPS, and losing it is acceptable because the data is rebuilt each run.
option_breakdown.C: Filestore is a shared network file system, slower than a local device for one VM's scratch data.
option_breakdown.D: A Persistent Disk is durable network storage, which scratch data doesn't need, and its IOPS are lower.

questions.title: Forty VMs sharing one directory tree
questions.summary: Filestore is managed NFS; shared POSIX access from many clients is impossible on a block device.
questions.question: Forty VMs in a render farm must read and write the same directory tree concurrently over NFS. Which storage should you provision?

options.A: A zonal Persistent Disk
options.B: A regional Persistent Disk
options.C: Filestore
options.D: Google Cloud Hyperdisk

explanation.summary: Filestore is the managed NFS service, and shared POSIX access from many clients is something a block device cannot provide.

option_breakdown.A: A Persistent Disk is a block device, not a shared NFS file system for forty VMs.
option_breakdown.B: A regional disk is still a block device with a single writer; it adds zone replication, not sharing.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Filestore is the managed NFS service, and shared POSIX access from many clients is something a block device can't provide.
option_breakdown.D: Hyperdisk is block storage; it doesn't give forty VMs one shared, writable directory tree.

questions.title: 300,000 IOPS without over-buying capacity
questions.summary: Hyperdisk decouples provisioned IOPS and throughput from capacity.
questions.question: A demanding OLTP database needs 300,000 IOPS on a 2 TB volume. Provisioning far more capacity than needed purely to obtain the IOPS is unacceptable. Which storage should you attach?

options.A: Local SSD
options.B: Filestore
options.C: A zonal Persistent Disk
options.D: Hyperdisk Extreme

explanation.summary: Hyperdisk decouples provisioned IOPS and throughput from capacity, which is the only way to buy the performance without over-buying the size.

option_breakdown.A: Local SSD is lost when the VM stops, which is unacceptable for a database's only copy.
option_breakdown.B: Filestore is a shared NFS file system, not a block volume for an OLTP database.
option_breakdown.C: Persistent Disk performance is tied to disk size and type, and even its fastest type tops out well below 300,000 IOPS per disk.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Hyperdisk Extreme lets you provision IOPS independently of capacity, so a 2 TB volume can have 300,000 IOPS.

questions.title: Cheapest durable boot disk for a stateless VM
questions.summary: Because the instance is disposable, a zonal PD avoids paying for cross-zone replication.
questions.question: A stateless web server needs a durable boot disk at the lowest cost. If the zone fails, the instance is simply recreated from an image elsewhere. Which storage should you attach?

options.A: A zonal Persistent Disk
options.B: A regional Persistent Disk
options.C: Google Cloud Hyperdisk
options.D: Local SSD

explanation.summary: Because the instance is disposable and rebuilt from an image, a standard zonal Persistent Disk gives durable boot storage without paying for cross-zone replication.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The instance is disposable and rebuilt from an image, so a zonal Persistent Disk gives durable boot storage without paying for cross-zone replication.
option_breakdown.B: Replicating the boot disk to a second zone costs more, and the instance is rebuilt from an image anyway.
option_breakdown.C: Hyperdisk bills for provisioned performance that a small web server's boot disk doesn't need.
option_breakdown.D: Local SSD can't be a boot disk, and it isn't durable.

questions.title: Traffic triples every weekday morning
questions.summary: The MIG autoscaler adds and removes instances against a target metric.
questions.question: Traffic to a web tier running in a managed instance group triples every weekday morning and falls away overnight. The group must add and remove VMs automatically as CPU load changes. What should you configure?

options.A: Autohealing with an application health check.
options.B: An autoscaler with a target CPU utilisation.
options.C: A rolling update to a larger machine type.
options.D: A regional group spread across three zones.

explanation.summary: The managed instance group autoscaler adds and removes instances against a target metric such as CPU utilisation or load balancer capacity, which is what a diurnal traffic pattern needs.

option_breakdown.A: Autohealing replaces unhealthy VMs; it doesn't change how many there are.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The MIG autoscaler adds and removes instances to hold a target such as CPU utilisation, which follows a daily traffic pattern.
option_breakdown.C: Bigger machines raise capacity all day, including overnight, and don't respond to load.
option_breakdown.D: Spreading across zones adds resilience, not capacity that follows demand.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig --region=us-central1 \
  --min-num-replicas=3 --max-num-replicas=30 --target-cpu-utilization=0.6

questions.title: VM alive but application hung
questions.summary: Autohealing detects a live VM with a dead application and recreates the instance.
questions.question: VMs in a managed instance group occasionally keep running while the application inside them hangs. The hung VMs must be detected and recreated automatically. What should you configure?

options.A: A regional group spread across three zones.
options.B: A health check on the load balancer's backend service only.
options.C: Autohealing on the group, with an application health check.
options.D: An autoscaler with a target CPU utilisation.

explanation.summary: Autohealing uses an application-level health check to detect exactly this case — a live VM with a dead application — and recreates the instance.

option_breakdown.A: Spreading across zones doesn't detect a hung application.
option_breakdown.B: The load balancer stops sending traffic to failing VMs, but it never recreates them.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Autohealing uses an application health check to detect a running VM with a hung application, and recreates it.
option_breakdown.D: The autoscaler changes the number of VMs with load; a hung VM may even look idle.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --region=us-central1 \
  --health-check=app-hc --initial-delay=180

questions.title: Patch 30 instances without losing capacity
questions.summary: A rolling update with maxSurge creates replacements before removing old instances.
questions.question: A patched image, in a new instance template, must be rolled out to the 30 VMs of a managed instance group without ever dropping below the current serving capacity. What should you configure?

options.A: A rolling update with max unavailable 3 and max surge 0.
options.B: A rolling replace of all VMs from the current template.
options.C: Set the new template on the group without starting an update.
options.D: A rolling update with max surge 3 and max unavailable 0.

explanation.summary: A rolling update with max surge above zero and max unavailable at zero creates each replacement before removing an old VM, so capacity never drops.

option_breakdown.A: Taking up to three VMs out at a time, with none added first, drops below current capacity.
option_breakdown.B: Replace recreates VMs from the template the group already uses, so the patch isn't applied.
option_breakdown.C: Without an update, existing VMs keep the old image; only VMs created later use the new template.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Surge VMs are created first, and none of the current VMs is taken away until its replacement is ready.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig \
  --region=us-central1 --version=template=web-tpl-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0

questions.title: Serving tier spans zones automatically
questions.summary: A regional MIG distributes instances across zones and redistributes after a zonal failure.
questions.question: A serving tier in a managed instance group must keep running if one zone in the region fails, and its VMs should be redistributed across the remaining zones automatically. What should you configure?

options.A: A regional managed instance group.
options.B: A zonal managed instance group with autohealing.
options.C: Two zonal groups in different zones, resized by hand after a failure.
options.D: A zonal managed instance group with an autoscaler.

explanation.summary: A regional managed instance group distributes instances across the zones of a region and redistributes them automatically after a zonal failure.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A regional MIG spreads VMs across the region's zones and redistributes them automatically after a zonal failure.
option_breakdown.B: Autohealing recreates VMs in the same zone, which doesn't help when the zone is down.
option_breakdown.C: The tier survives, but redistributing capacity is manual, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.D: An autoscaler adds VMs in the group's one zone, which is the zone that failed.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed create web-mig --template=web-tpl \
  --size=6 --region=us-central1

questions.title: Canary a version to 10 percent
questions.summary: A canary rollout is a second version on the MIG with a percentage target size.
questions.question: A new version of an app is packaged in a new instance template, v2. Before a full rollout, it must run on only 10% of the VMs in the app's managed instance group, so it can be observed. What should you do?

options.A: Create a second managed instance group from v2 and scale it by hand.
options.B: Start a rolling update with v2 as a canary version, targeting 10% of the group.
options.C: Edit the current instance template so 10% of VMs use the v2 image.
options.D: Run a rolling replace on 10% of the group's VMs.

explanation.summary: A canary is a second version with a target size on the same MIG; the updater keeps 10% of instances on v2 and the rest on v1 until you promote.

option_breakdown.A: It can work, but you'd wire up load balancing and keep the 10% proportion by hand; the MIG updater does this for you.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A canary is a second version with a target size in the same MIG; the updater keeps 10% of VMs on v2 and the rest on v1 until you promote it.
option_breakdown.C: Instance templates can't be edited; you create a new template instead.
option_breakdown.D: Replace recreates VMs from the template the group already uses, so it doesn't introduce v2.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig \
  --region=us-central1 --version=template=web-tpl-v1 \
  --canary-version=template=web-tpl-v2,target-size=10%

questions.title: Branch office connected this week
questions.summary: HA VPN provisions in minutes, encrypts with IPsec, and needs no physical circuit.
questions.question: A branch office needs private connectivity to Google Cloud within the week, with modest bandwidth and encryption in transit as the priority. Which option should you choose?

options.A: Dedicated Interconnect
options.B: Partner Interconnect
options.C: HA VPN
options.D: VPC Network Peering

explanation.summary: HA VPN can be configured in minutes, encrypts traffic with IPsec, and carries the bandwidth a branch office needs without any physical provisioning.

option_breakdown.A: Dedicated Interconnect takes weeks to provision, needs presence in a colocation facility, and isn't encrypted by default.
option_breakdown.B: A provider must provision the connection, which rarely fits in a week, and it isn't encrypted by default.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. HA VPN can be set up in an afternoon, encrypts traffic with IPsec, and carries the modest bandwidth a branch office needs.
option_breakdown.D: Peering connects two VPC networks; it can't reach an office.

questions.title: 20 Gbps with predictable latency
questions.summary: Dedicated Interconnect provides 10/100 Gbps circuits with deterministic performance.
questions.question: Kestrel Genomics must move several petabytes from its data centre over the next year, sustaining 20 Gbps to Google Cloud with predictable latency. Its racks already sit in a colocation facility where Google has a point of presence, and its routers support 10 Gbps optics. Which connection should you choose?

options.A: VPC Network Peering
options.B: Cross-Cloud Interconnect
options.C: HA VPN
options.D: Dedicated Interconnect

explanation.summary: Dedicated Interconnect provides 10 or 100 Gbps circuits with deterministic performance, and being present in a colocation facility is precisely its prerequisite.

option_breakdown.A: Peering connects two VPC networks; it can't reach a data centre.
option_breakdown.B: Cross-Cloud Interconnect connects Google Cloud to other cloud providers, not to your own data centre.
option_breakdown.C: Each HA VPN tunnel carries about 3 Gbps over the internet, so 20 Gbps means many tunnels, with internet latency.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Dedicated Interconnect gives 10 or 100 Gbps circuits with predictable performance, and presence in a colocation facility is its prerequisite.

questions.title: 1 Gbps without colocation presence
questions.summary: Partner Interconnect bridges the last mile through a service provider at sub-10 Gbps.
questions.question: The company needs 1 Gbps of private connectivity to Google Cloud that does not cross the public internet. It is not present in any Google colocation facility and cannot become so. Which option should you choose?

options.A: Partner Interconnect
options.B: HA VPN
options.C: Dedicated Interconnect
options.D: VPC Network Peering

explanation.summary: Partner Interconnect exists for organisations that cannot meet Google in a colocation facility: a service provider bridges the last mile at sub-10 Gbps bandwidths.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Partner Interconnect is for organisations that can't meet Google in a colocation facility: a service provider supplies the connection, at capacities from 50 Mbps.
option_breakdown.B: HA VPN could carry 1 Gbps, but over the public internet, which is ruled out.
option_breakdown.C: Dedicated Interconnect requires presence in a colocation facility, which the company can't have.
option_breakdown.D: Peering connects two VPC networks; it can't reach an on-premises network.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute interconnects attachments partner create dc-attach \
  --region=us-central1 --router=cr-1 --edge-availability-domain=availability-domain-1

questions.title: Encrypted backup path for an Interconnect
questions.summary: HA VPN over the internet is the standard Interconnect failover, arbitrated by Cloud Router BGP priorities.
questions.question: An existing Dedicated Interconnect must have an encrypted backup path that can carry production traffic if the circuit fails, taking over only on failure. What should you deploy?

options.A: A second Dedicated Interconnect circuit in the same facility, unencrypted.
options.B: HA VPN, with its routes advertised at a lower priority than the Interconnect's.
options.C: Partner Interconnect as the only backup.
options.D: Cloud NAT on the Interconnect's region.

explanation.summary: HA VPN is IPsec-encrypted, and BGP route priorities (MED) make it carry traffic only when the Interconnect is down.

option_breakdown.A: A second circuit adds capacity but not encryption, and it shares the facility's failure domain.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. HA VPN is IPsec-encrypted, and BGP route priorities (MED) make it carry traffic only when the Interconnect is down.
option_breakdown.C: Partner Interconnect, like Dedicated, is not encrypted by default.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud NAT gives private VMs outbound internet access; it connects nothing to on-premises.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute routers update cr-1 --region=us-central1  # set advertised route priority on the VPN peer

questions.title: Reviewable multi-environment infrastructure
questions.summary: Terraform with remote state is the standard declarative multi-environment workflow.
questions.question: Networking, projects and databases must be defined in version control, reviewed by pull request, and applied identically to dev, staging and production. What should you use?

options.A: Config Connector, managing Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.
options.B: Helm charts.
options.C: Terraform with the Google provider, state stored in a Cloud Storage bucket.
options.D: gcloud scripts that engineers run in each environment.

explanation.summary: Terraform with remote state in Cloud Storage is the standard declarative workflow for reviewable, repeatable multi-environment infrastructure.

option_breakdown.A: Config Connector needs a Kubernetes cluster to run in, and the projects and networks come before any cluster.
option_breakdown.B: Helm deploys Kubernetes applications; it doesn't create projects, VPCs or databases.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Terraform with remote state in Cloud Storage is the standard declarative workflow for reviewable infrastructure applied the same way to every environment.
option_breakdown.D: Scripts are imperative and keep no state, so environments drift and a pull request can't show the planned change.

questions.title: Provision cloud resources via kubectl
questions.summary: Config Connector exposes Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes CRDs.
questions.question: A platform team wants application teams to request Cloud SQL instances and Pub/Sub topics by submitting Kubernetes manifests to the cluster they already use daily. What should you use?

options.A: Helm charts that template the manifests.
options.B: Configure the resources by hand in the Google Cloud console.
options.C: Terraform with the Google provider, state stored in a Cloud Storage bucket.
options.D: Config Connector, managing Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.

explanation.summary: Config Connector exposes Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources, so the existing manifest-and-kubectl workflow becomes the provisioning interface.

option_breakdown.A: Helm templates Kubernetes objects; without something that reconciles Google Cloud resources, it creates no Cloud SQL instance.
option_breakdown.B: Console changes can't be submitted as manifests or reviewed, and they drift.
option_breakdown.C: Terraform works from outside the cluster with its own files; it doesn't accept Kubernetes manifests.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Config Connector exposes Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources, so the existing manifest-and-kubectl workflow becomes the provisioning interface.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f sqlinstance.yaml   # kind: SQLInstance, sql.cnrm.cloud.google.com/v1beta1

questions.title: One app, four clusters, different values
questions.summary: Helm values files parameterise one packaged Kubernetes application per environment.
questions.question: The same Kubernetes application must be deployed to four GKE clusters with different replica counts, hostnames and resource limits, from a single packaged definition. What should you use?

options.A: Helm charts.
options.B: Terraform with the Google provider, state stored in a Cloud Storage bucket.
options.C: Config Connector, managing Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.
options.D: Four copies of the manifests, one per GKE cluster.

explanation.summary: Helm's values files are designed for exactly this per-environment parameterisation of a single packaged Kubernetes application.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A Helm chart packages the application once, and a values file per cluster sets its replicas, hostnames and limits.
option_breakdown.B: Terraform provisions infrastructure; it isn't a packaging format for a Kubernetes application.
option_breakdown.C: Config Connector creates Google Cloud resources from Kubernetes; it doesn't package an application.
option_breakdown.D: Copies drift apart, which is what a single packaged definition avoids.

questions.title: Greenfield landing zone on Terraform
questions.summary: Fabric FAST is Google's opinionated staged Terraform landing-zone framework.
questions.question: A brand new organisation needs a complete landing zone: hierarchy, billing, networking and security baselines. The team wants to start from a staged, opinionated Terraform framework rather than writing every module themselves. What should you use?

options.A: Helm charts.
options.B: Fabric FAST, the opinionated Terraform landing-zone framework.
options.C: Configure the resources by hand in the Google Cloud console.
options.D: Terraform with the Google provider, writing each module yourself.

explanation.summary: Fabric FAST is the opinionated, staged Terraform framework Google publishes for exactly this greenfield landing-zone bootstrap.

option_breakdown.A: Helm deploys Kubernetes applications, not organisations, billing or networks.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Fabric FAST is a staged, opinionated Terraform framework for bootstrapping a landing zone.
option_breakdown.C: Hand-built console setups can't be reviewed or reproduced.
option_breakdown.D: It works, but the team would write every module, which is what it wants to avoid.

questions.title: Run a container on each new object
questions.summary: Eventarc has a first-class Cloud Storage source delivering finalised events to Cloud Run.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service must run whenever an object is finalised in a specific Cloud Storage bucket, with no polling, no infrastructure to run, and the fewest resources to configure yourself. How should you wire the event flow?

options.A: A Cloud Storage notification to a Pub/Sub topic, with a push subscription to the service.
options.B: A Pub/Sub topic with workers pulling from a subscription.
options.C: A Cloud Scheduler job that invokes the service every minute.
options.D: An Eventarc trigger for the bucket's finalised events.
