explanation.summary: Eventarc has a first-class Cloud Storage source and delivers the finalised event to Cloud Run in CloudEvents format with no polling.

option_breakdown.A: It works, but you create and maintain the notification, topic and subscription yourself; one Eventarc trigger sets this up for you.
option_breakdown.B: Pull workers must run all the time and poll, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.C: A schedule polls, and it reacts up to a minute late.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Eventarc has a Cloud Storage source and delivers each finalised event to Cloud Run, with one trigger and no polling.

questions.title: React to VM deletions via audit logs
questions.summary: Eventarc can trigger on Cloud Audit Log entries filtered by service and method name.
questions.question: A service must react whenever any VM instance is deleted anywhere in the project, using the audit trail as the event source. How should you wire this?

options.A: An Eventarc trigger on Cloud Audit Logs entries for Compute Engine instance deletions.
options.B: A Cloud Scheduler job every minute that lists instances and compares them with the last run.
options.C: A log-based metric counting deletions, with an alerting policy that emails the team.
options.D: A Cloud Storage notification to Pub/Sub, subscribed by the service.

explanation.summary: Eventarc turns Admin Activity audit-log entries into events, filtered by service and method name, and delivers each one to the service.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Eventarc turns Admin Activity audit-log entries into events, filtered by service and method name, and delivers each one to the service.
option_breakdown.B: Polling is late, wasteful and misses short-lived instances between runs.
option_breakdown.C: An alert tells people; it does not make the service react to each deletion.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Storage notifications report object changes in a bucket, not VM deletions.

questions.title: Existing topic to a scale-to-zero service
questions.summary: A push subscription posts each message to the Cloud Run URL, allowing scale from zero.
questions.question: An internal application already publishes order events to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Run service must process each one as it arrives and scale to zero when the topic is quiet. How should you wire this?

options.A: A Cloud Run job that drains a pull subscription every five minutes.
options.B: A push subscription on the topic that posts to the service's URL.
options.C: A pull subscription that the Cloud Run service reads from.
options.D: A Cloud Scheduler job that invokes the service every minute.

explanation.summary: A push subscription posts each message to the Cloud Run URL, which lets the service scale from zero on demand without a worker holding a pull connection open.

option_breakdown.A: Messages wait up to five minutes, so they aren't processed as they arrive.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A push subscription posts each message to the Cloud Run URL, so the service scales up from zero when messages arrive and back down when the topic is quiet.
option_breakdown.C: A service scaled to zero isn't running to pull, and pulling keeps instances alive.
option_breakdown.D: A schedule invokes the service whether or not there are messages, up to a minute late.

questions.title: Workers control their own throughput
questions.summary: Pull subscriptions let the consumer set throughput and acknowledgement timing.
questions.question: A fleet of long-running workers on Compute Engine must process a backlog at a rate they control, acknowledging messages only after slow downstream writes succeed. How should you wire this?

options.A: A push subscription to an HTTP endpoint on the workers.
options.B: A Cloud Tasks queue that dispatches to the workers.
options.C: A pull subscription that the workers read from.
options.D: An Eventarc trigger that sends each message to a Cloud Run service.

explanation.summary: Pull subscriptions let the consumer set its own throughput and acknowledgement timing, which is what flow control for a slow downstream requires.

option_breakdown.A: With push, Pub/Sub decides the delivery rate; the workers can only slow it by failing requests.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Tasks pushes at a rate set on the queue, and producers would have to create tasks instead of publishing.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Pull subscriptions let the consumer set its own throughput and acknowledge each message only after the slow write succeeds.
option_breakdown.D: That moves the work to Cloud Run, away from the Compute Engine workers, and delivery is pushed.

questions.title: Nightly reconciliation at 02:00
questions.summary: A fixed daily time is a schedule, not an event; Cloud Scheduler invokes with an OIDC token.
questions.question: A reconciliation job must run at 02:00 every day against a Cloud Run service, authenticated. How should you wire this?

options.A: Create an Eventarc trigger that routes the event to the service.
options.B: Publish to a Pub/Sub topic and configure a push subscription to the service endpoint.
options.C: Publish to a Pub/Sub topic and have workers pull from a subscription.
options.D: Create a Cloud Scheduler job that invokes the service.

explanation.summary: A fixed daily time is a schedule, not an event, and Cloud Scheduler invokes the service with an OIDC token at that time.

option_breakdown.A: Eventarc reacts to events from sources; a time of day isn't one of them.
option_breakdown.B: A push subscription delivers what someone publishes, and nothing publishes at 02:00 unless something is scheduled to.
option_breakdown.C: Pulling needs a running consumer polling, and still something to publish at 02:00.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A fixed daily time is a schedule, not an event, and Cloud Scheduler calls the service with an OIDC token at that time.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud scheduler jobs create http nightly-recon --schedule='0 2 * * *' \
  --uri=https://recon-xyz.a.run.app --location=us-central1 \
  --oidc-service-account-email=SA@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: Custom CUDA kernels must run unchanged
questions.summary: Custom CUDA is GPU-specific; TPUs use a different programming model entirely.
questions.question: A research team runs custom CUDA kernels for scientific simulation and needs the code to run in the cloud without modification. What should you choose?

options.A: Attach GPUs to the instances.
options.B: Use Cloud TPUs.
options.C: Use CPU-only instances with more vCPUs.
options.D: Use compute-optimised C3 instances.

explanation.summary: Custom CUDA is GPU-specific; TPUs run a different programming model and cannot execute CUDA kernels.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Custom CUDA is GPU-specific; TPUs run a different programming model and cannot execute CUDA kernels.
option_breakdown.B: TPUs use a different programming model through frameworks such as JAX; they can't run CUDA kernels.
option_breakdown.C: CUDA kernels need an NVIDIA GPU; more vCPUs don't run them.
option_breakdown.D: C3 instances are fast CPUs, but CUDA kernels still need an NVIDIA GPU.

questions.title: Large JAX model, best price-performance
questions.summary: TPUs are purpose-built for large-scale matrix computation in supported frameworks.
questions.question: A large transformer model is trained in JAX across many chips. The team wants accelerators that are purpose-built for large-scale matrix computation in JAX, at the lowest cost per training run. What should you choose?

options.A: Use Hyperdisk ML volumes to serve the training data to the workers.
options.B: Use Cloud TPUs.
options.C: Use general-purpose CPU instances only.
options.D: Attach GPUs to the instances.

explanation.summary: TPUs are purpose-built for large-scale matrix computation in supported frameworks such as JAX and TensorFlow, where they beat GPUs on price-performance.

option_breakdown.A: Hyperdisk ML is storage for serving data to many VMs; it doesn't do the computation.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. TPUs are purpose-built for large-scale matrix computation in frameworks such as JAX and TensorFlow, and Google positions them for training price-performance at this scale.
option_breakdown.C: CPU-only training of a large transformer would take far longer and cost more per run.
option_breakdown.D: GPUs run JAX well, but for large-scale training in a framework built on XLA, TPUs are the purpose-built option.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create train-node --zone=us-central2-b \
  --accelerator-type=v4-8 --version=tpu-vm-v4-base

questions.title: Global anycast IP for lowest latency
questions.summary: Global anycast and backbone transit to the nearest edge are Premium Tier features.
questions.question: A global consumer application must give users on every continent the lowest possible latency and needs a single global anycast IP address. Which option should you choose?

options.A: Standard Tier, with a regional external load balancer on each continent.
options.B: Cloud DNS geolocation routing to a regional IP on each continent.
options.C: Use the Premium network service tier.
options.D: Use the Standard network service tier.

explanation.summary: Global anycast addresses and backbone transit to the nearest edge are Premium Tier features; Standard Tier is regional only.

option_breakdown.A: That gives one IP per region, not a single global anycast address, and Standard Tier traffic crosses the public internet.
option_breakdown.B: Geolocation routing hands out several regional IPs, not one anycast address.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Global anycast addresses and backbone transit to the nearest edge are Premium Tier features; Standard Tier is regional only.
option_breakdown.D: Standard Tier is regional: no global anycast IP, and traffic enters Google's network near the region, not near the user.

questions.title: Large regional egress, cost dominant
questions.summary: Standard Tier egresses locally at a lower price, right for regional latency-tolerant traffic.
questions.question: A batch pipeline pushes large volumes of egress from one region to a partner in the same country. Egress cost dominates the bill and the traffic is latency-tolerant. Which option should you choose?

options.A: Use the Premium network service tier.
options.B: Cloud CDN in front of the pipeline's endpoint.
options.C: Cloud NAT for the pipeline's VMs.
options.D: Use the Standard network service tier.

explanation.summary: Standard Tier egresses from the local region at a lower price, which is the right trade when the traffic is regional and latency-tolerant.

option_breakdown.A: Premium Tier carries traffic on Google's backbone and costs more, which a latency-tolerant regional transfer doesn't need.
option_breakdown.B: A CDN caches content read repeatedly by users; a one-way bulk push doesn't benefit.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud NAT gives private VMs outbound access; it doesn't lower egress prices and adds its own processing charge.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Standard Tier egress leaves Google's network near the region at a lower price, the right trade for regional, latency-tolerant traffic.

questions.title: Accelerators will not fix a serial bottleneck
questions.summary: Accelerators only help parallel numerical work; a serialised query must be fixed in the database.
questions.question: A web application on Compute Engine is slow. Profiling shows the cause is a single-threaded database query, with no parallel numerical work anywhere in the request path. What should you do to speed up requests?

options.A: Optimise the query and the database; keep general-purpose CPU instances.
options.B: Attach GPUs to the web servers.
options.C: Move the web tier to Cloud TPU VMs.
options.D: Add more web server instances.

explanation.summary: Accelerators speed up parallel numerical work. A slow, serial query is fixed in the query or the database, and the web tier stays on general-purpose CPUs.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The bottleneck is a serial query, so the fix is in the query or the database, not in hardware acceleration.
option_breakdown.B: GPUs speed up parallel numerical work, and there is none in the request path.
option_breakdown.C: TPUs accelerate matrix computation for ML frameworks; they do nothing for a database query.
option_breakdown.D: More web servers send the same slow query to the same database.

questions.title: Unbounded user uploads served worldwide
questions.summary: Cloud Storage gives unlimited capacity, HTTPS serving and native lifecycle management.
questions.question: An application must store an unbounded number of user-uploaded files, serve them worldwide over HTTPS, and age them into cheaper classes over time. What should you use?

options.A: Filestore
options.B: Cloud Storage
options.C: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes
options.D: Google Cloud Managed Lustre

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage is the object store with effectively unlimited capacity, direct HTTPS serving and native object lifecycle management.

option_breakdown.A: Filestore is an NFS file share with a fixed capacity; it doesn't serve files over HTTPS or age them into cheaper classes.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Storage is object storage with effectively unlimited capacity, HTTPS access and lifecycle rules that move objects to cheaper classes.
option_breakdown.C: NetApp Volumes is managed file storage for NFS and SMB, not an HTTPS object store.
option_breakdown.D: Managed Lustre is a parallel file system for HPC scratch, not durable storage served to users.

questions.title: Unmodifiable app needs a POSIX mount
questions.summary: Filestore presents a standard NFS mount for unmodified POSIX applications.
questions.question: A lift-and-shift application needs a shared POSIX file system, mounted read-write by several VMs, with modest throughput. It cannot be rewritten to use an object API. What should you use?

options.A: Google Cloud Managed Lustre
options.B: A bucket mounted on each VM with Cloud Storage FUSE.
options.C: Filestore
options.D: A Persistent Disk attached to every VM.

explanation.summary: Filestore presents a standard NFS mount, which is what an unmodified POSIX application requires.

option_breakdown.A: Managed Lustre is a parallel file system for HPC throughput, more than a modest general-purpose share needs.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Storage FUSE is not fully POSIX: it lacks, for example, file locking and concurrent-writer semantics.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Filestore provides a standard NFS share that several VMs mount read-write, which is what an unmodified POSIX application needs.
option_breakdown.D: A Persistent Disk can be attached read-write to only one VM at a time (multi-writer is limited to specific cases), and it isn't a shared file system.

questions.title: SMB shares with snapshots and replication
questions.summary: NetApp Volumes provides managed SMB alongside NFS with enterprise snapshot and replication.
questions.question: A migrated enterprise workload needs SMB shares, snapshot-based restore and cross-region replication managed by the platform rather than by scripts. What should you use?

options.A: A Windows file server VM, with snapshot and replication scripts.
options.B: Cloud Storage
options.C: Filestore
options.D: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes

explanation.summary: NetApp Volumes is the managed service providing SMB alongside NFS with enterprise snapshot and replication features built in.

option_breakdown.A: It provides SMB, but snapshots and replication would be scripts, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Storage is object storage; it doesn't present SMB shares.
option_breakdown.C: Filestore serves NFS, not SMB.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. NetApp Volumes is the managed service that provides SMB alongside NFS, with snapshots and cross-region replication built in.

questions.title: HPC scratch at hundreds of GB/s
questions.summary: Managed Lustre is the parallel filesystem built for HPC scratch at that throughput.
questions.question: An HPC simulation needs hundreds of gigabytes per second of aggregate throughput to shared scratch storage across thousands of cores. What should you use?

options.A: Google Cloud Managed Lustre
options.B: Filestore
options.C: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes
options.D: A Persistent Disk on each compute node.

explanation.summary: Managed Lustre is the parallel filesystem built for HPC scratch at this throughput, which NFS-based services cannot reach.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Managed Lustre is a parallel file system built for HPC scratch at this aggregate throughput.
option_breakdown.B: Filestore is NFS, whose throughput falls far short of hundreds of gigabytes per second.
option_breakdown.C: NetApp Volumes is enterprise file storage, not a parallel file system for thousands of cores.
option_breakdown.D: Separate disks aren't shared, and the simulation needs one shared scratch space.

questions.title: Two petabytes from another cloud, on a schedule
questions.summary: Storage Transfer Service is the managed, resumable, scheduled cross-cloud transfer service.
questions.question: Two petabytes of objects must move from another cloud provider into Cloud Storage on a repeating schedule, with retries and integrity checking handled for you. What should you use?

options.A: Transfer Appliance
options.B: Storage Transfer Service
options.C: Upload with the gcloud storage command-line client.
options.D: BigQuery Data Transfer Service

explanation.summary: Storage Transfer Service is the managed, resumable, scheduled service for cross-cloud and on-premises transfers at this scale.

option_breakdown.A: Transfer Appliance is for shipping data from your own premises on hardware, not for repeated pulls from another cloud.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Storage Transfer Service is the managed, scheduled service for cloud-to-cloud transfers, with retries and integrity checks.
option_breakdown.C: The CLI runs from one machine; scheduling, retries and verification of two petabytes would be yours to build.
option_breakdown.D: It loads data into BigQuery tables, not objects into Cloud Storage.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud transfer jobs create s3://source-bucket gs://dest-bucket \
  --source-creds-file=aws.json --schedule-repeats-every=24h

questions.title: One-off 40 GB upload from a workstation
questions.summary: The gcloud storage client performs parallel, resumable uploads for one-off transfers.
questions.question: An engineer needs to copy a 40 GB directory from their workstation to a bucket once, resuming automatically if the connection drops. What should they use?

options.A: Storage Transfer Service, with an agent on the workstation.
options.B: Transfer Appliance
options.C: Upload with the gcloud storage command-line client.
options.D: A Cloud Storage FUSE mount, copying with cp.

explanation.summary: The gcloud storage client performs parallel, resumable uploads and is the right tool for a one-off transfer from a single machine.

option_breakdown.A: Agent-based transfers are built for large or recurring jobs; installing agents for one 40 GB copy is far more setup.
option_breakdown.B: Transfer Appliance ships hardware for very large offline transfers, not 40 GB.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The gcloud storage client uploads in parallel and resumes interrupted uploads, which suits a one-off copy from one machine.
option_breakdown.D: FUSE turns the copy into ordinary file writes, so an interrupted cp doesn't resume where it stopped.

questions.title: Twelve interchangeable stateless replicas
questions.summary: A Deployment is the controller for interchangeable stateless replicas with native rolling updates.
questions.question: A stateless API must run twelve identical replicas that can be replaced freely during rolling updates. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: Create a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate.
options.B: Create a DaemonSet.
options.C: Create a Deployment.
options.D: Create a Job or CronJob.

explanation.summary: A Deployment is the controller for interchangeable stateless replicas and manages rolling updates and rollbacks natively.

option_breakdown.A: A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable name and its own volume, which is unnecessary overhead for stateless replicas.
option_breakdown.B: A DaemonSet runs exactly one Pod per node, right for node agents and wrong for scaling application replicas.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A Deployment is the controller for interchangeable stateless replicas and manages rolling updates and rollbacks natively.
option_breakdown.D: Jobs run a workload to completion rather than serving traffic continuously.

questions.title: Clustered database needing stable identity
questions.summary: StatefulSets provide ordinal stable names and per-Pod PersistentVolumeClaims.
questions.question: A clustered database running on GKE needs each replica to keep a stable network identity and its own persistent volume across restarts and rescheduling. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: A Job
options.B: A Deployment with one PersistentVolumeClaim
options.C: A DaemonSet with hostPath volumes
options.D: A StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate

explanation.summary: StatefulSets provide ordinal, stable Pod names and per-Pod PersistentVolumeClaims, which clustered databases depend on.

option_breakdown.A: A Job runs to completion; a database must keep serving.
option_breakdown.B: Every replica would share the same claim, and Deployment Pods get random names, not stable identities.
option_breakdown.C: hostPath ties data to a node, and a DaemonSet runs one Pod per node rather than a set number of replicas.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. StatefulSets give Pods stable ordinal names and a PersistentVolumeClaim each, which clustered databases depend on.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f statefulset.yaml   # kind: StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates

questions.title: Log agent on every node including new ones
questions.summary: A DaemonSet schedules one Pod per node automatically, including newly added nodes.
questions.question: A log-collection agent must run on every node of a GKE Standard cluster, including nodes added later by the cluster autoscaler. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: A DaemonSet
options.B: A Deployment with one replica per node and Pod anti-affinity
options.C: A static Pod manifest copied to each node
options.D: A StatefulSet with one replica per node

explanation.summary: A DaemonSet schedules one Pod per node automatically, including on newly added nodes, which is the node-agent pattern.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A DaemonSet schedules one Pod on every node automatically, including nodes added later.
option_breakdown.B: Anti-affinity spreads the replicas, but the replica count doesn't follow the node count when the autoscaler adds nodes.
option_breakdown.C: GKE manages the nodes, so new nodes don't get your manifest, and files on a node can be replaced.
option_breakdown.D: A StatefulSet gives Pods stable identities; it doesn't place exactly one on each node.

questions.title: One-off migration that must retry then stop
questions.summary: A Job runs Pods until a specified number complete successfully, then finishes.
questions.question: On GKE, a data migration must run once to completion, retrying on failure, and then stop permanently. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: A StatefulSet
options.B: A Job
options.C: A CronJob
options.D: A Deployment

explanation.summary: A Job runs Pods until the required number complete successfully, retries failures up to its backoff limit, and then finishes.

option_breakdown.A: A StatefulSet keeps Pods running and restarts them when they exit.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A Job retries until the migration succeeds and then stops.
option_breakdown.C: A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule, so the migration would run again.
option_breakdown.D: Deployment Pods always restart when they exit, so the migration would run repeatedly.

questions.title: Two services, one hostname, path routing
questions.summary: An Ingress or Gateway provisions an external ALB with path rules and managed certificates.
questions.question: Two Services in a GKE cluster must be reachable from the internet under one hostname, routed by URL path, with a Google-managed TLS certificate. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: A NodePort Service for each Service
options.B: A LoadBalancer Service for each Service
options.C: An Ingress or a Gateway
options.D: A ClusterIP Service for each Service

explanation.summary: An Ingress (or Gateway) provisions an external Application Load Balancer with path rules and can attach a Google-managed certificate.

option_breakdown.A: NodePort opens a port on every node; it gives no hostname, path routing or managed certificate.
option_breakdown.B: Each LoadBalancer Service gets its own layer 4 load balancer and IP, with no path routing or TLS termination.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An Ingress or Gateway provisions an external Application Load Balancer with path rules, and can attach a Google-managed certificate.
option_breakdown.D: ClusterIP is reachable only inside the cluster.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml   # with a ManagedCertificate annotation

questions.title: Expose a non-HTTP TCP service externally
questions.summary: A Service of type LoadBalancer provisions a layer 4 load balancer for arbitrary TCP.
questions.question: A non-HTTP TCP service running in a GKE cluster must be reachable from outside the cluster on a fixed port. Which Kubernetes object should you create?

options.A: An Ingress
options.B: A ClusterIP Service
options.C: A headless Service
options.D: A LoadBalancer Service

explanation.summary: A Service of type LoadBalancer provisions a layer 4 load balancer, which is what a non-HTTP protocol requires.

option_breakdown.A: GKE Ingress provisions an HTTP(S) load balancer, which can't carry a non-HTTP protocol.
option_breakdown.B: A ClusterIP Service gets an address that only Pods and nodes inside the cluster can reach.
option_breakdown.C: A headless Service gives DNS records for Pods inside the cluster; it doesn't expose anything externally.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A LoadBalancer Service provisions a layer 4 network load balancer, which carries any TCP protocol on a fixed port.

questions.title: kubectl reports no configured cluster
questions.summary: get-credentials writes the cluster endpoint and auth config into kubeconfig.
questions.question: A GKE cluster exists. A newly provisioned workstation has gcloud installed and authenticated, but every kubectl command reports that no cluster is configured. What should you run?

options.A: gcloud container clusters get-credentials
options.B: gcloud auth login, a second time
options.C: gcloud config set compute/region
options.D: The installer for gke-gcloud-auth-plugin

explanation.summary: get-credentials writes the cluster's endpoint and authentication configuration into kubeconfig, which is the prerequisite for any kubectl command.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. get-credentials writes the cluster's endpoint and authentication settings into kubeconfig, which kubectl needs before anything else.
option_breakdown.B: gcloud is already authenticated; kubectl reads kubeconfig, which still has no cluster in it.
option_breakdown.C: This sets a gcloud default; it doesn't write kubeconfig.
option_breakdown.D: The plugin is needed to authenticate, but a missing plugin produces a different error; kubeconfig still has no cluster.

questions.title: Specialise a generic image at boot
questions.summary: A startup script in metadata specialises a generic image without rebuilding it.
questions.question: Every VM in a managed instance group must install the monitoring agent and fetch its configuration at first boot, while the base image stays generic and is not rebuilt per role. What should you use?

options.A: A custom image built for each role
options.B: A shutdown script in instance metadata
options.C: A custom metadata key holding the agent's configuration
options.D: A startup script in instance metadata

explanation.summary: A startup script in metadata runs on boot and is the supported way to specialise a generic image without rebuilding it.

option_breakdown.A: Rebuilding images per role is what the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.B: A shutdown script runs when the VM stops, not at boot.
option_breakdown.C: Metadata only stores values; nothing installs the agent unless a script reads them.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A startup script in metadata runs at boot, which is the supported way to specialise a generic image without rebuilding it.

questions.title: Uniform instances for a managed group
questions.summary: An instance template is the required input to a MIG and fixes those properties.
questions.question: A managed instance group must be created so every instance it launches has the same machine type, disks, network tags and service account. What must you create first?

options.A: Create an instance template.
options.B: A machine image of a configured VM
options.C: Create a custom image from the configured disk.
options.D: A sole-tenant node template

explanation.summary: An instance template is the required input to a managed instance group and fixes exactly these properties for every instance it creates.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An instance template is the required input to a managed instance group, and it fixes these properties for every VM the group creates.
option_breakdown.B: A machine image backs up a VM's configuration and disks; a managed instance group is created from an instance template, not from a machine image.
option_breakdown.C: An image provides the boot disk only, not the machine type, tags or service account.
option_breakdown.D: A node template describes sole-tenant hosts, not the VMs a group launches.

questions.title: SSH access tied to IAM identities
questions.summary: OS Login binds POSIX accounts to IAM identities, so revoking the role removes SSH access.
questions.question: Linux SSH access must be granted and revoked through the same IAM identities used everywhere else, and access must disappear when an employee is offboarded. What should you do?

options.A: Add each engineer's public key to project-wide metadata.
options.B: Enable OS Login and grant the engineers' group the OS Login role.
options.C: Give each engineer a service-account key for SSH.
options.D: Share one Linux account's private key among the team through Secret Manager.

explanation.summary: OS Login creates Linux accounts from Google identities, so SSH access is an IAM grant: remove the grant or suspend the user and access ends everywhere.

option_breakdown.A: Metadata keys stay valid until someone removes them by hand; offboarding does not touch them.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. OS Login creates Linux accounts from Google identities, so SSH access is an IAM grant: remove the grant or suspend the user and access ends everywhere.
option_breakdown.C: Service-account keys are not SSH credentials and are exactly the long-lived secret to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: A shared key cannot be revoked for one person and leaves no per-user audit trail.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata enable-oslogin=TRUE
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member='user:eng@example.com' --role='roles/compute.osLogin'

questions.title: Two-factor on production Linux logins
questions.summary: OS Login supports two-factor authentication as a project or instance setting.
questions.question: Security requires two-factor authentication on interactive Linux logins to production instances. What should you configure?

options.A: Enable OS Login with two-step verification.
options.B: Deploy a bastion host with an external IP and connect through it.
options.C: Enable interactive access to the serial console.
options.D: Connect through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding.

explanation.summary: OS Login supports two-factor authentication as a project or instance setting, which metadata-based SSH keys cannot offer.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. OS Login can require two-step verification on SSH logins as a project or instance setting, which metadata-based SSH keys can't.
option_breakdown.B: A bastion adds a hop, but SSH keys alone still log in with one factor.
option_breakdown.C: The serial console is a recovery path; enabling it adds a login route rather than a second factor.
option_breakdown.D: IAP adds an IAM check on the network path, but the Linux login itself still needs a second factor, which OS Login provides.

questions.title: Show reviewers the infrastructure diff
questions.summary: terraform plan produces exactly that diff against current state.
questions.question: A reviewer must be able to see precisely which infrastructure resources a change will add, modify and destroy, before anything happens. What should the pipeline do?

options.A: Run terraform plan and then terraform apply from the pipeline.
options.B: Define the steps in a Cloud Build configuration and trigger it from the repository.
options.C: Use Cloud Deploy to promote the release through a delivery pipeline.
options.D: Run terraform apply -auto-approve on every merge.

explanation.summary: terraform plan produces exactly that diff against current state, which is why plan-before-apply is the reviewable infrastructure workflow.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. terraform plan produces exactly that diff against current state, which is why plan-before-apply is the reviewable infrastructure workflow.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Build can run the steps, but on its own it shows the reviewer no infrastructure diff.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Deploy promotes application releases; it doesn't show infrastructure changes.
option_breakdown.D: Auto-approve applies changes with no plan for anyone to review first.

questions.title: Hosting an agent without building serving infrastructure
questions.summary: Agent Runtime is the managed runtime for AI agents: scaling, sessions, memory, identity and tracing included.
questions.question: A team has built a customer-support agent with the Agent Development Kit. They need managed hosting that provides scaling, conversation sessions and memory, a service identity, and tracing, and they do not want to build or operate the serving infrastructure themselves. Where should they deploy it?

options.A: A GKE Standard cluster with a Deployment and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
options.B: A Compute Engine VM running the agent under systemd.
options.C: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
options.D: A Cloud Run function triggered over HTTP.

explanation.summary: Agent Runtime (formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine) is the guide's compute answer for AI agents: you deploy the agent built with ADK, LangGraph or similar, and the platform supplies scaling, sessions, memory, identity, tracing and logging.

option_breakdown.A: GKE can host an agent, but the team would build and run the serving, session and memory layers themselves.
option_breakdown.B: A VM is the most operational work of all and provides none of the agent features.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. It is purpose-built to host agents with sessions, memory and tracing managed for you.
option_breakdown.D: Functions are stateless request handlers; sessions and memory would have to be built separately.

explanation.gcloud_command: # From the Agent Platform SDK: package the ADK agent and deploy it to Agent Runtime in a region

questions.title: Monthly OS patching across hundreds of VMs
questions.summary: VM Manager patch deployments schedule OS patching and report compliance across a fleet without SSH.
questions.question: Three hundred Linux VMs across several projects must receive operating-system patches every month, in a maintenance window, with a report of which instances succeeded. Nobody should SSH into instances to do it. What should you configure?

options.A: A monthly VM Manager patch deployment for the target instances.
options.B: A startup script that runs the package manager's upgrade command.
options.C: A rolling replacement of every instance through a managed instance group.
options.D: unattended-upgrades on each VM, configured over SSH once.

explanation.summary: VM Manager's OS patch management runs patch jobs now or on a schedule (patch deployments), targets instances by zone, label or name, supports pre- and post-patch scripts and reboot settings, and reports per-instance results — no SSH involved.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It schedules, targets and reports patching across the fleet.
option_breakdown.B: Startup scripts run only at boot, so long-running VMs would never be patched.
option_breakdown.C: Most of these VMs are not in managed instance groups, and replacement is not patching.
option_breakdown.D: Per-VM configuration needs SSH, gives no central report and drifts.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute os-config patch-deployments create monthly-patch \
  --file=patch-deployment.yaml   # schedule, instance filter, reboot config

questions.title: Patch job reports that no agent was found
questions.summary: VM Manager needs the OS Config API, the enable-osconfig metadata and the OS Config agent on each instance.
questions.question: A new VM Manager patch job skips several instances and reports that the OS Config agent is not reporting. The instances run supported images. What should you check and fix?

options.A: That the instances are in a managed instance group, which VM Manager requires.
options.B: That each instance has an external IP address so the patch service can reach it.
options.C: That the Service Usage API is enabled in the organisation's billing project.
options.D: That the OS Config API, the metadata flag and the agent are all in place.

explanation.summary: VM Manager works through the OS Config agent on each VM. It needs the OS Config API enabled in the project, VM Manager turned on through the enable-osconfig metadata key, and a running agent whose service account can reach the API (Private Google Access or NAT is enough).

option_breakdown.A: Any VM can be managed; group membership is irrelevant.
option_breakdown.B: Agents call out to the API; instances do not need external IPs.
option_breakdown.C: Service Usage is not the missing piece; the OS Config API and agent are.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. An instance reports to VM Manager only when the OS Config API is enabled, the instance has enable-osconfig=TRUE metadata, and the OS Config agent is installed and running.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud services enable osconfig.googleapis.com
gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata=enable-osconfig=TRUE

questions.title: Stop one VM accepting project-wide SSH keys
questions.summary: block-project-ssh-keys on an instance makes it ignore keys stored in project metadata.
questions.question: A contractor's public key was added to project metadata so they could reach the development VMs. One VM in the project holds sensitive data and must not accept that key, while the project metadata stays unchanged. OS Login is not used in this project. What should you do?

options.A: Delete the contractor's key from project metadata and add it to every other instance instead.
options.B: Set the block-project-ssh-keys metadata value to TRUE on the sensitive instance.
options.C: Remove the external IP address from the sensitive instance.
options.D: Create a firewall rule denying port 22 from the contractor's office range.

explanation.summary: With metadata-based SSH keys, instances accept both project-wide and instance-level keys unless the instance sets block-project-ssh-keys. That one setting excludes every project-level key from that VM while leaving the rest of the project untouched. (OS Login is the long-term fix: access by IAM instead of keys.)

option_breakdown.A: The requirement was to leave project metadata unchanged, and per-instance copies multiply the key.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. It removes project-wide keys from that single instance only.
option_breakdown.C: The contractor can still reach it through IAP or from inside the VPC with the key.
option_breakdown.D: An IP-based rule does not follow the person, and the key would still be accepted from anywhere else.

questions.title: kubectl cannot find the GKE authentication plugin
questions.summary: Current kubectl authenticates to GKE through gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, installed as a gcloud component.
questions.question: On a new workstation you install kubectl and run `gcloud container clusters get-credentials`. Every kubectl command then fails with an error that `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` was not found. What should you do?

options.A: Reinstall kubectl from the Kubernetes project's release page.
options.B: Grant yourself roles/container.admin on the project.
options.C: Install the gke-gcloud-auth-plugin component.
options.D: Delete ~/.kube/config and copy the cluster's CA certificate into it by hand.

explanation.summary: kubectl no longer contains GKE-specific authentication; it calls the gke-gcloud-auth-plugin binary to obtain credentials from gcloud. Installing the plugin fixes the error; get-credentials already wrote a kubeconfig that uses it.

option_breakdown.A: The kubectl binary is fine; the plugin it calls is missing.
option_breakdown.B: The failure is a missing local binary, not a permission denial.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin (or the matching OS package) installs the credential plugin that kubectl calls for GKE.
option_breakdown.D: Hand-editing kubeconfig does not provide credentials and would be overwritten.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin
gcloud container clusters get-credentials prod --region=REGION

questions.title: Moving Kafka applications without rewriting clients
questions.summary: Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs real Kafka clusters, so existing Kafka clients work unchanged.
questions.question: Dozens of on-premises applications produce to and consume from Apache Kafka topics with Kafka client libraries and consumer groups. They must move to Google Cloud without changing producer or consumer code, and the team no longer wants to operate brokers or ZooKeeper. What should you choose?

options.A: Pub/Sub, replacing the Kafka client calls with the Pub/Sub client library.
options.B: Kafka on a self-managed GKE StatefulSet.
options.C: Dataflow, reading and writing Kafka topics.
options.D: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka.

explanation.summary: Managed Service for Apache Kafka provides Kafka clusters that Google operates, speaking the open-source Kafka protocol, so existing clients, topics and consumer groups carry over. Pub/Sub is the serverless native alternative, but choosing it means rewriting against its API.

option_breakdown.A: Pub/Sub would work only after rewriting every producer and consumer, which the requirement rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Self-managed Kafka keeps exactly the broker operations the team wants to stop doing.
option_breakdown.C: Dataflow processes streams; it is not a Kafka-compatible broker.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Kafka-compatible and operated for you.

questions.title: Serverless messaging for a new Cloud Run application
questions.summary: For new serverless designs, Pub/Sub offers pay-per-use global messaging with push delivery and no capacity to size.
questions.question: A new application built on Cloud Run needs asynchronous messaging between services. Messages should be pushed to a Cloud Run endpoint, the team doesn't want to size or pay for idle broker capacity, and there is no existing Kafka code. What should you choose?

options.A: Pub/Sub, with push subscriptions.
options.B: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka.
options.C: Memorystore for Redis lists used as queues.
options.D: Bigtable tables polled by each service.

explanation.summary: Pub/Sub is serverless and global, bills per use, and can push each message to an HTTPS endpoint such as a Cloud Run service. Managed Kafka is the right choice when Kafka compatibility is the requirement, but it means provisioning cluster capacity.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Serverless, push-capable and billed per use — the fit for a greenfield Cloud Run design.
option_breakdown.B: Managed Kafka still has provisioned cluster capacity, and nothing here needs the Kafka protocol.
option_breakdown.C: A cache used as a queue lacks delivery guarantees, retries and push.
option_breakdown.D: Polling a database adds latency and cost and reinvents a message queue.

questions.title: Replace a BigQuery table from a CSV with a header
questions.summary: bq load with --replace and --skip_leading_rows overwrites a table from a headed CSV in Cloud Storage.
questions.question: Each night a CSV file with one header row arrives in a Cloud Storage bucket. It must fully replace the contents of an existing BigQuery table that has a fixed schema. What should the nightly job run?

options.A: A query that inserts rows selected directly from the file's URI.
options.B: A load job that overwrites the table and skips the header row.
options.C: A copy of the file into the table with gcloud storage cp.
options.D: An external table definition over the file.

explanation.summary: A load job from Cloud Storage is the standard way to bring a file into a native table. --replace truncates the table before writing (the default appends), and --skip_leading_rows=1 ignores the header.

option_breakdown.A: A query can't read a raw file URI unless an external table is defined first, and an INSERT appends rather than replaces.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A load job with replace and one skipped leading row (bq load --replace --source_format=CSV --skip_leading_rows=1) overwrites the table from the file.
option_breakdown.C: gcloud storage copies objects between storage locations; a BigQuery table isn't one.
option_breakdown.D: An external table queries the file in place; the native table's contents stay as they were.

questions.title: A 15-minute RPO for objects across two regions
questions.summary: Dual-region buckets with turbo replication replicate 100% of new objects to both regions within 15 minutes.
questions.question: Objects in a bucket must survive the loss of an entire region, and newly written objects must exist in the second region within 15 minutes. Data must stay in two named European regions. What should you configure?

options.A: A regional bucket with Object Versioning enabled.
options.B: A multi-region EU bucket with default replication.
options.C: A dual-region bucket in the two regions, with turbo replication.
options.D: Two regional buckets synchronised hourly by Storage Transfer Service.

explanation.summary: A dual-region bucket keeps data in two specific regions. Default replication is asynchronous with a 12-hour target for 99.9% of objects; turbo replication adds a 15-minute recovery point objective for all newly written objects.

option_breakdown.A: Versioning protects against overwrites, not against the region being unavailable.
option_breakdown.B: Multi-region placement is not two named regions, and default replication has no 15-minute guarantee.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Two chosen regions with a 15-minute replication objective.
option_breakdown.D: An hourly sync cannot meet a 15-minute RPO and adds a pipeline to operate.

questions.title: Recover Cloud SQL in another region if the primary region fails
questions.summary: A cross-region read replica is Cloud SQL's disaster-recovery path: promote it if the primary region is lost.
questions.question: A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance already runs in a high-availability configuration in europe-west1. The business now requires that the database can be brought back in another region if the whole region is lost, with a recovery point of minutes, not a day. What should you add?

options.A: A cross-region read replica in europe-west4, promoted if needed.
options.B: A second zone for the standby, since high availability already spans regions.
options.C: Automated backups with the retention raised to 365 days.
options.D: An hourly export to a Coldline bucket in the same region.

explanation.summary: High availability protects against a zone failure only; the standby is in the same region. A cross-region read replica is continuously updated by replication and can be promoted to a standalone primary, giving a recovery point measured in seconds to minutes.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Continuous replication to another region, promotable when needed.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud SQL high availability is regional; its standby is in another zone of the same region.
option_breakdown.C: Backup retention changes how far back you can go, not how quickly you recover in a new region.
option_breakdown.D: An export in the same region does not survive the regional outage and loses up to an hour of data.

questions.title: A Firestore database that survives a regional outage
questions.summary: Firestore's multi-region locations replicate synchronously across regions; the location is fixed at creation.
questions.question: A mobile application's Firestore database must stay available with no failover action if one Google Cloud region becomes unavailable. The database has not been created yet. What should you do?

options.A: Create it in a regional location and schedule daily exports to another region.
options.B: Create it in a regional location, then change it to multi-region when traffic grows.
options.C: Create two regional databases and write every document to both from the application.
options.D: Create the database in a multi-region location such as nam5 or eur3.

explanation.summary: Firestore multi-region locations replicate data synchronously across regions, so reads and writes continue through a regional outage without any action. A database's location cannot be changed after creation, which is why the choice has to be made now.

option_breakdown.A: Exports allow a slow restore; they do not keep the database available.
option_breakdown.B: The location of a Firestore database is permanent once created.
option_breakdown.C: Dual writes from the application are fragile and still leave consistency to you.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Synchronous multi-region replication, chosen at creation time.

questions.title: Egress allowed only to a partner hostname whose IPs change
questions.summary: Cloud NGFW Standard adds FQDN objects to network firewall policy rules, tracking a hostname's changing addresses.
questions.question: Workloads in a VPC may send traffic to the internet only to api.partner.example.com, whose IP addresses change several times a week. All other internet egress must be denied. What should you configure?

options.A: A VPC firewall egress rule allowing the partner's current IP addresses, updated by a weekly script.
options.B: A network firewall policy allowing the partner's FQDN, above a deny-all rule.
options.C: Cloud NAT configured to translate only the partner's addresses.
options.D: A Cloud DNS response policy that resolves every other name to 0.0.0.0.

explanation.summary: FQDN objects (Cloud NGFW Standard) let a firewall-policy rule match a domain name; Cloud NGFW resolves it and keeps the address list current. Combined with a lower-priority deny-all egress rule, only that partner is reachable.

option_breakdown.A: Addresses change more often than a weekly script runs, and VPC firewall rules cannot use FQDNs.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The FQDN object follows the hostname's addresses; the deny rule blocks everything else.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud NAT provides address translation, not destination filtering.
option_breakdown.D: DNS tricks are bypassed by any workload that connects to an IP address directly.

questions.title: Enforce one rule centrally and delegate the rest
questions.summary: A hierarchical firewall policy rule can deny centrally and use goto_next to hand other traffic to project rules.
questions.question: Security must block SSH from the internet (0.0.0.0/0) in every project, with no project able to override it. Every other allow or deny decision must stay with each project's own firewall rules. What should you configure on the organisation node?

options.A: A hierarchical firewall policy that allows all traffic, so projects inherit an open default.
options.B: An organisation policy constraint that disables firewall rule creation in projects.
options.C: A hierarchical policy denying internet SSH, with goto_next for the rest.
options.D: A VPC firewall rule in each project denying tcp:22, with the priority set to 0.

explanation.summary: Hierarchical policies are evaluated before a network's own rules. A deny cannot be overridden lower down, and goto_next passes everything the organisation does not decide to the next level — the projects' rules and network policies.

option_breakdown.A: An allow at the top pre-empts the projects' own decisions, the opposite of delegation.
option_breakdown.B: Blocking rule creation removes the projects' ability to make any decision at all.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Enforced centrally where it matters, delegated everywhere else.
option_breakdown.D: Project-level rules can be edited or deleted by project owners, so the control is not guaranteed.

questions.title: Only the platform team may place a VM in a firewall group
questions.subtopic: Secure Tags and Service Accounts in Rules
questions.summary: Secure tags need an IAM role to attach, so editing a VM cannot move it into a firewall rule's scope.
questions.question: Developers hold instanceAdmin on their projects and can edit network tags. Security wants only the platform team to be able to place a VM into the 'pci' group that a firewall rule allows to reach the payment database. What should the firewall rule target?

options.A: A secure tag value, with tagUser granted only to the platform team.
options.B: The network tag 'pci', with a naming convention documented for developers.
options.C: An IP range reserved for PCI workloads in the same subnet.
options.D: All instances in the network, with an IAM condition restricting who can create VMs.

explanation.summary: Attaching a secure tag value to a VM requires roles/resourcemanager.tagUser on that value (plus rights on the VM). Network tags can be added by anyone who can edit the instance. Firewall policies select sources and targets by secure tags, so the IAM control on the tag becomes the control on firewall scope.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. IAM on the tag value decides who can place a VM into the rule's scope.
option_breakdown.B: Anyone who can edit the VM can add a network tag, which is exactly the gap.
option_breakdown.C: Addresses inside a shared subnet are assigned by whoever creates the VM, so this is no control at all.
option_breakdown.D: Targeting every instance allows all of them, whoever created them.

questions.title: A firewall policy rule that never matches a network tag
questions.subtopic: Secure Tags and Service Accounts in Rules
questions.summary: Firewall policies select by secure tags, not network tags; network tags work only in VPC firewall rules.
questions.question: An engineer moved an ingress rule from VPC firewall rules into a global network firewall policy and set its target to the network tag 'web' used on the web servers. The rule never matches. What is the cause?

options.A: Global network firewall policies apply only to egress traffic.
options.B: The policy must be attached at the folder level before rules take effect.
options.C: Network tags take up to 24 hours to propagate into firewall policies.
options.D: Firewall policies can't use network tags; a secure tag is needed.

explanation.summary: Network tags are a VPC firewall rule feature. Firewall policies — hierarchical, global and regional network — select targets and sources by secure tags or service accounts, so a rule written against the old network tag has nothing to match.

option_breakdown.A: Network firewall policies hold both ingress and egress rules.
option_breakdown.B: Global network firewall policies are associated with a VPC network, not a folder.
option_breakdown.C: There is no propagation delay; the selector type is unsupported.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Secure tags replace network tags inside firewall policies.

questions.title: Self-service from governed architecture templates
questions.summary: Application Design Center lets platform teams publish approved, Terraform-backed templates for self-service deployment.
questions.question: A platform team wants application developers to design and deploy new applications only from approved, reusable architecture templates that the platform team publishes, using a visual (AI-assisted) canvas, with the result registered as an application in App Hub. What should they use?

options.A: Gemini CLI, with a prompt file that describes the approved architectures.
options.B: Application Design Center.
options.C: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds that flag unapproved resources after creation.
options.D: A shared folder of gcloud scripts that developers copy and edit.

explanation.summary: Application Design Center is built for governed self-service: platform administrators publish Terraform-backed templates, developers compose applications from them on a canvas (with Gemini assistance), deploy, and the result is registered in App Hub.

option_breakdown.A: An AI terminal agent generates code on request; it does not enforce a catalogue of approved designs.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Governed templates, a visual canvas and App Hub registration are exactly its purpose.
option_breakdown.C: Detection after the fact is not self-service from approved designs.
option_breakdown.D: Copied scripts drift immediately and carry no governance.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Application Design Center > Templates (admins publish) / Applications (developers deploy)

questions.title: An AI agent in the terminal that writes and runs infrastructure code
questions.summary: Gemini CLI (now the Antigravity CLI) is the terminal agent that reads code, writes IaC and runs commands with approval.
questions.question: An engineer wants an AI agent in their terminal that can read the repository, write the Terraform for a new Cloud Run service, and run the gcloud and terraform commands — asking for approval before each command. What fits?

options.A: Gemini Cloud Assist in the Google Cloud console.
options.B: Application Design Center.
options.C: Gemini CLI
options.D: Cloud Shell's built-in code editor.

explanation.summary: Gemini CLI — whose capabilities Google moved into the Antigravity CLI in 2026 — is an agent that runs in your terminal: it reads files, writes code and infrastructure definitions, and executes shell commands with your approval.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud Assist lives in the console and analyses your cloud resources; it is not a terminal agent over a repository.
option_breakdown.B: Application Design Center is a console canvas for governed templates, not a coding agent.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A terminal-native agent working on the local repository.
option_breakdown.D: An editor is not an agent; it does not plan or run anything by itself.

explanation.gcloud_command: gemini   # then: 'write Terraform for a Cloud Run service in this repo and plan it'

questions.title: Applying infrastructure code an AI assistant generated
questions.summary: AI-generated IaC is a draft: it goes through review, a plan and the normal pipeline before it reaches production.
questions.question: Gemini Cloud Assist has generated a Terraform configuration for a new production network. The team normally applies infrastructure from a pipeline running as a deploy service account. What should they do with the generated code?

options.A: Apply it from the engineer's laptop immediately, because generated code has already been validated.
options.B: Paste the resulting resources into the console by hand so nothing runs automatically.
options.C: Ask the assistant to apply it directly to production with an Owner grant, to save time.
options.D: Commit it, review it and its plan in a pull request, and let the pipeline apply it.

explanation.summary: Generated commands and infrastructure code are drafts. They follow the same path as human-written code — version control, review of the plan, apply by the pipeline's least-privilege identity — and an assistant acts with the permissions of whoever uses it, so it should not be granted broad production rights.

option_breakdown.A: Nothing about generation guarantees correctness, and laptop applies bypass the review trail.
option_breakdown.B: Manual console changes lose the code and create drift.
option_breakdown.C: Broad grants to an assistant widen the blast radius and skip review.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Same review and pipeline as any other change.

explanation.gcloud_command: terraform plan -out=tfplan   # attached to the pull request; the pipeline applies after approval

questions.title: An agent-first development platform
questions.summary: Google Antigravity is an agent-first development platform where agents carry out multi-step tasks across editor, terminal and browser.
questions.question: A development team wants an agent-first desktop development platform in which AI agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across the editor, the terminal and a browser, with the developer reviewing the results. What should they adopt?

options.A: Google Antigravity.
options.B: Cloud Workstations.
options.C: Gemini Cloud Assist.
options.D: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

explanation.summary: Google Antigravity is the agent-first development platform named in the guide: agents plan and execute development work across the editor, terminal and browser. The other options are a hosted dev environment, a console assistant, and a runtime for hosting your own agents.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An agentic development platform for developers.
option_breakdown.B: Workstations provide managed development machines; they are not an agent platform.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Assist helps with Google Cloud resources in the console, not with multi-step coding tasks.
option_breakdown.D: Agent Runtime hosts agents you build for your users; it is not a development tool.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Install Google Antigravity; agents work across editor, terminal and browser

questions.title: Patching without taking out a zone
questions.summary: A patch deployment's rollout settings (zone by zone, disruption budget) limit how many VMs patch at once.
questions.question: A weekly VM Manager patch deployment covers 300 VMs in three zones. Last week every VM in a zone rebooted at the same moment and a service went down. Patching must now proceed one zone at a time, with at most 10% of a zone's VMs disrupted at once. What should you change?

options.A: The deployment's rollout settings: zone by zone, 10% disruption budget.
options.B: Split the VMs into 300 patch deployments, one per VM.
options.C: Disable reboots in the patch configuration so patches never apply.
options.D: Replace the patch deployment with a cron job on each VM.

explanation.summary: Patch deployments and patch jobs have rollout options that process zones one at a time and cap the number or percentage of VMs disrupted concurrently.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Patch deployments and patch jobs have rollout options that process zones one at a time and cap the number or percentage of VMs disrupted concurrently.
option_breakdown.B: Hundreds of deployments are unmanageable and still start together.
option_breakdown.C: Some patches need a reboot to take effect; suppressing it leaves VMs unpatched.
option_breakdown.D: Per-VM cron is the assembled version of a managed feature, with no rollout control.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# patch deployment: rollout: { mode: ZONE_BY_ZONE, disruptionBudget: { percent: 10 } }
gcloud compute os-config patch-deployments create weekly --file=weekly.yaml

questions.title: An emergency patch on production VMs, now
questions.summary: A VM Manager patch job applies patches immediately to VMs selected by labels or zones; patch deployments are schedules.
questions.question: A critical kernel update must be applied today to every Linux VM labelled env=prod, without waiting for the fleet's monthly patch window and without logging in to each VM. VM Manager is enabled. What should you do?

options.A: Run a VM Manager patch job now, filtered on the label env=prod.
options.B: Edit the monthly patch deployment's schedule and wait for the next run.
options.C: Recreate every production VM from the latest public image.
options.D: Run gcloud compute ssh on each VM with an update script.

explanation.summary: A patch job runs immediately against the VMs matched by its filter, with rollout controls and a per-VM report; patch deployments are the recurring schedule.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A patch job runs immediately against the VMs matched by its filter, with rollout controls and a per-VM report; patch deployments are the recurring schedule.
option_breakdown.B: Changing a schedule still waits for a future run, and affects every later run too.
option_breakdown.C: Recreating VMs is disruptive and loses anything not baked into the image.
option_breakdown.D: Logging in to each VM is the manual work VM Manager replaces.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute os-config patch-jobs execute \
  --instance-filter-group-labels="env=prod" --display-name="kernel hotfix"

questions.title: Pointing kubectl at a different cluster
questions.summary: kubectl talks to its current context; switch contexts (or run get-credentials) to target another cluster.
questions.question: You ran get-credentials earlier for two GKE clusters, staging and prod. kubectl commands now reach prod, but you need to work on staging for the next hour. What should you do?

options.A: Run gcloud config set project to the staging project.
options.B: Run kubectl config use-context with the staging cluster's context name.
options.C: Delete the prod entry from kubeconfig, then run kubectl again.
options.D: Run gcloud container clusters resize on staging to activate it.

explanation.summary: kubeconfig holds one context per cluster; use-context switches the active one without touching the others.

option_breakdown.A: gcloud's active project does not change kubectl's current context.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubeconfig holds one context per cluster; use-context switches the active one without touching the others.
option_breakdown.C: Deleting the entry works but loses the prod configuration you will need again.
option_breakdown.D: Resizing changes node count; it has nothing to do with which cluster kubectl talks to.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context gke_PROJECT_europe-central2_staging

questions.title: Stop typing -n shop on every command
questions.summary: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace sets the default namespace of the current context.
questions.question: You spend the day working in namespace shop of one GKE cluster, and every kubectl command needs -n shop added. How do you make shop the default namespace for your current kubectl context?

options.A: Set a default namespace on the current kubeconfig context.
options.B: Label the shop namespace as the default namespace.
options.C: Switch to a kubeconfig context named shop.
options.D: Limit your RBAC permissions to the shop namespace.

explanation.summary: A kubeconfig context carries a default namespace; set-context --current changes it for the context in use.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A kubeconfig context carries a default namespace; kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop changes it for the context in use.
option_breakdown.B: Labels are metadata; kubectl's default namespace comes from the context, not from a label.
option_breakdown.C: Contexts are named per cluster and user; a context named shop doesn't exist unless you create one.
option_breakdown.D: RBAC limits what you may do; commands still default to the context's namespace.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace

questions.title: A partner's engineer needs SSH through OS Login
questions.summary: Users from outside the organisation need roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser at the organisation level.
questions.question: OS Login is enforced on all VMs. An engineer from a partner company, whose Google account is outside your organisation, was granted roles/compute.osLogin on one VM but still cannot log in. What else is required?

options.A: An SSH key for the user in the VM's instance metadata.
options.B: OS Login External User for that user, granted on the organisation.
options.C: roles/compute.osAdminLogin instead of roles/compute.osLogin.
options.D: A Cloud Identity account for the user in the partner's domain.

explanation.summary: OS Login admits users from outside the organisation only when they also hold OS Login External User on the organisation; it must be granted there, not on the project.

option_breakdown.A: With OS Login enabled, metadata keys are ignored.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. OS Login admits users from outside the organisation only when they also hold OS Login External User on the organisation; it must be granted there, not on the project.
option_breakdown.C: Admin login adds sudo; it does not lift the external-user restriction.
option_breakdown.D: Your organisation cannot create accounts in another company's domain, and the partner's identity is already a Google account.

questions.title: OS Login to a VM that runs as a service account
questions.summary: OS Login to a VM with an attached service account also needs Service Account User on that account.
questions.question: An engineer holds roles/compute.osLogin on a VM that runs as app@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com, but OS Login refuses the SSH session. Other VMs without a service account work. Which additional grant fixes it with least privilege?

options.A: roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on the project for the engineer.
options.B: roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 on the project for the engineer.
options.C: roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on that service account.
options.D: roles/owner on the VM for the engineer.

explanation.summary: Logging in to a VM that runs as a service account lets you act through it, so OS Login also requires Service Account User on that service account — granted on the account itself.

option_breakdown.A: Token Creator is for minting tokens, and a project-level grant covers every service account.
option_breakdown.B: Instance Admin manages VMs; it is broader and still does not grant actAs on the account.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Logging in to a VM that runs as a service account lets you act through it, so OS Login also requires Service Account User on that service account — granted on the account itself.
option_breakdown.D: Owner is far beyond the need.

questions.title: Accelerating a video transcoding farm
questions.summary: Transcoding and rendering are general-purpose parallel work for GPUs; TPUs are for tensor maths.
questions.question: A media company transcodes thousands of video files a night with FFmpeg, using NVIDIA's hardware encoding support. It wants to cut the time per file. Which accelerator should it choose?

options.A: NVIDIA GPUs attached to the transcoding VMs.
options.B: Cloud TPUs, which offer the best price-performance for accelerated work.
options.C: Local SSDs on the transcoding VMs.
options.D: Memory-optimised machine types without accelerators.

explanation.summary: Video encoding runs on GPU hardware encoders through NVIDIA's libraries; TPUs are ASICs for large matrix and tensor operations and do not run this work.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Video encoding runs on GPU hardware encoders through NVIDIA's libraries; TPUs are ASICs for large matrix and tensor operations and do not run this work.
option_breakdown.B: TPUs lead on large-scale XLA training and serving, not on video encoding.
option_breakdown.C: Faster disks help I/O, not the encoding computation.
option_breakdown.D: More memory does not accelerate an encoding workload.

questions.title: PyTorch training on TPUs without a rewrite
questions.summary: PyTorch runs on TPUs through PyTorch/XLA; JAX is not required.
questions.question: A team trains a large language model in PyTorch with no custom CUDA kernels. It has read that TPUs offer better price-performance at its scale but believes it would first have to rewrite the model in JAX. What is true?

options.A: TPUs run only JAX, so the rewrite is unavoidable.
options.B: PyTorch runs on TPUs through PyTorch/XLA, with no JAX rewrite.
options.C: TPUs run only TensorFlow, so the model must be converted.
options.D: PyTorch can use TPUs only for inference, never for training.

explanation.summary: TPUs execute XLA-compiled programs; JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch (through PyTorch/XLA) all target XLA, so the PyTorch model can train on TPUs.

option_breakdown.A: JAX is one supported framework, not the only one.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. TPUs execute XLA-compiled programs; JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch (through PyTorch/XLA) all target XLA, so the PyTorch model can train on TPUs.
option_breakdown.C: TensorFlow is supported, but so are JAX and PyTorch.
option_breakdown.D: PyTorch/XLA supports training as well as inference.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create train-1 --zone=ZONE --accelerator-type=v5litepod-8 \
  --version=v2-alpha-tpuv5-lite

questions.title: An upload trigger that never fires
questions.summary: Cloud Storage triggers need the Cloud Storage service agent to hold Pub/Sub Publisher.
questions.question: A Cloud Run function was deployed with an Eventarc trigger on object finalized events for a bucket in the same region. Uploads succeed, but the function never runs and the trigger shows no deliveries. What should you check first?

options.A: That the bucket uses the Standard storage class.
options.B: That the function allows unauthenticated invocations.
options.C: That the Cloud Storage service agent can publish to Pub/Sub.
options.D: That object versioning is enabled on the bucket.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage events travel through Pub/Sub, and it is the Cloud Storage service agent that publishes them; without Pub/Sub Publisher no event ever reaches Eventarc.

option_breakdown.A: The storage class of the bucket does not affect event delivery.
option_breakdown.B: Eventarc invokes the function with its trigger service account; the function need not be public.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Storage events travel through Pub/Sub, and it is the Cloud Storage service agent that publishes them; without Pub/Sub Publisher no event ever reaches Eventarc.
option_breakdown.D: Versioning has nothing to do with finalized events.

explanation.gcloud_command:
SA=$(gcloud storage service-agent --project=PROJECT_ID)
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=serviceAccount:$SA --role=roles/pubsub.publisher

questions.title: A container batch that must run to completion nightly
questions.summary: Cloud Run jobs run tasks to completion, in parallel with retries, triggered on a schedule.
questions.question: A containerised export processes 200 files each night: each file is independent, a file can be retried if it fails, and nothing listens for requests. The team wants no servers and no Kubernetes cluster. What should they use?

options.A: A Cloud Run service that loops over the files when it receives a request.
options.B: A GKE Standard cluster with a CronJob.
options.C: A Compute Engine VM with a cron entry, running all day.
options.D: A Cloud Run job with 200 tasks, executed nightly by Cloud Scheduler.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run jobs execute tasks to completion — independently, in parallel, with retries — and Cloud Scheduler can run them on a timetable, with nothing running between runs.

option_breakdown.A: A service is for serving requests; long batch loops hit request timeouts and waste the model.
option_breakdown.B: A cluster works, but it is infrastructure the team said it does not want.
option_breakdown.C: An always-on VM pays for 24 hours to work for a few.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Cloud Run jobs execute tasks to completion — independently, in parallel, with retries — and Cloud Scheduler can run them on a timetable, with nothing running between runs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud run jobs create nightly-export --image=IMAGE --tasks=200 --max-retries=3 --region=REGION
gcloud run jobs execute nightly-export --region=REGION

questions.title: A new machine series rejects the disk type
questions.summary: Several newest machine series support only Hyperdisk; choose a Hyperdisk type for them.
questions.question: Creating a C4 VM with a 500 GB pd-balanced data disk fails with an error that the disk type is not supported by the machine type. The database needs durable block storage with tunable IOPS. What should you use?

options.A: A Local SSD, which every machine series supports.
options.B: A pd-ssd disk instead of pd-balanced.
options.C: A Filestore instance mounted over NFS.
options.D: A Hyperdisk Balanced disk.

explanation.summary: Some of the newest machine series, C4 among them, attach only Hyperdisk volumes; Hyperdisk Balanced gives durable block storage whose IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently of size.

option_breakdown.A: Local SSD data is lost when the VM stops, which fails the durability requirement.
option_breakdown.B: pd-ssd is another Persistent Disk type and is refused for the same reason.
option_breakdown.C: Filestore is a network file share, not the block device a database expects.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Some of the newest machine series, C4 among them, attach only Hyperdisk volumes; Hyperdisk Balanced gives durable block storage whose IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently of size.

questions.title: The same model weights on forty inference VMs
questions.summary: Hyperdisk ML is a read-only volume that many VMs can attach at once to load model data fast.
questions.question: Forty inference VMs each need to load the same 300 GB of model weights at start-up, as fast as possible. The weights change only when a new model version is released. Which storage fits best?

options.A: A Hyperdisk ML volume attached read-only to all forty VMs.
options.B: A separate Hyperdisk Balanced copy of the weights for each VM.
options.C: A regional Persistent Disk attached read-write to all forty VMs.
options.D: Local SSD on each VM, filled from Cloud Storage at every boot.

explanation.summary: Hyperdisk ML is designed for ML serving: one volume is attached read-only to many VMs and delivers very high aggregate read throughput.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Hyperdisk ML is designed for ML serving: one volume is attached read-only to many VMs and delivers very high aggregate read throughput.
option_breakdown.B: Forty copies multiply cost and add a copy step for every model release.
option_breakdown.C: A regional disk is for zone-level high availability and attaches read-write to one VM at a time.
option_breakdown.D: Refilling Local SSD at each boot slows start-up and loses the data on stop.

questions.title: A container job that runs to completion
questions.summary: Run-to-completion container work with no requests to serve is a Cloud Run job.
