questions.title: Cloud Run reachable only through the load balancer
questions.summary: Put Cloud Run behind an external Application Load Balancer with a serverless NEG, and set the service's ingress to internal and Cloud Load Balancing so the run.app URL stops accepting internet traffic.
questions.question: Pinecrest Tours serves a public booking API on Cloud Run. Security requires every request to pass through Cloud Armor, so the service's default run.app URL must stop accepting traffic from the internet, while customers keep reaching the API on the company's domain. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Configure Direct VPC egress for the service with all traffic routed to the VPC.
options.B: Create a VPC firewall rule that denies ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to the Cloud Run service.
options.C: Create an external Application Load Balancer with a serverless NEG for the service, and attach a Cloud Armor policy to its backend service.
options.D: Set the service's ingress to internal and Cloud Load Balancing.
options.E: Remove the allUsers Cloud Run Invoker binding from the service.

explanation.summary: Cloud Armor attaches to a load balancer's backend service, and a serverless NEG lets the load balancer front Cloud Run. The ingress setting decides which paths may reach the service; internal and Cloud Load Balancing closes the run.app URL to the internet.

option_breakdown.A: Egress settings control the service's outbound calls; they do nothing to who can reach it.
option_breakdown.B: VPC firewall rules apply to resources in the VPC, not to requests arriving at a Cloud Run service's URL.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The load balancer with a serverless NEG is where Cloud Armor applies to Cloud Run traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. This ingress setting rejects requests that don't come through a load balancer or the VPC, so the run.app URL stops serving the internet.
option_breakdown.E: Without allUsers, anonymous customers get 403 on every path, including the load balancer, so the public API breaks.

questions.title: Recreating VMs whose application hangs
questions.summary: MIG autohealing needs a health check on the group and a firewall rule that admits Google's health-check probe ranges.
questions.question: On Rydal Games' matchmaking servers, the process sometimes hangs while the VM stays running, so the VM keeps receiving traffic. The servers run in a regional managed instance group on a custom VPC that has only rules for its own subnets. Hung VMs must be recreated automatically. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Set the VMs' availability policy to restart them automatically after a failure.
options.B: Create an uptime check on the load balancer's address that alerts the on-call team.
options.C: Allow ingress from 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22 on the matchmaking port.
options.D: Install the Ops Agent on each VM so that process metrics reach Cloud Monitoring.
options.E: Create a health check for the matchmaking port and set it as the group's autohealing policy.

explanation.summary: Autohealing recreates a VM when the group's health check reports it unhealthy. The probes come from Google's health-check ranges, which a custom VPC with no matching rule would block, making every VM look unhealthy.

option_breakdown.A: Automatic restart reacts to a VM crash or host event; the VM here is still running.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check alerts people; it doesn't recreate anything in the group.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Without ingress from the probe ranges, the health checks fail on every VM.
option_breakdown.D: The Ops Agent collects metrics and logs; it has no part in autohealing.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. An autohealing policy with an application health check detects the hung process, not just a stopped VM.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed update mm-mig --region=REGION \
  --health-check=mm-hc --initial-delay=120

questions.title: HA VPN that qualifies for the 99.99% SLA
questions.summary: HA VPN reaches its 99.99% SLA only with two tunnels from both gateway interfaces and dynamic (BGP) routing through Cloud Router.
questions.question: Tilbury Steel is connecting a VPC to its plant's two on-premises VPN devices with HA VPN, and the link must qualify for the 99.99% availability SLA. Routes to new plant subnets should appear in the VPC without manual changes. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Use Classic VPN with route-based tunnels for the plant subnets.
options.B: Create one tunnel from interface 0, and add a second tunnel later if needed.
options.C: Add static routes for each plant subnet that point at the tunnels.
options.D: Use a Cloud Router with BGP sessions on the tunnels to exchange routes.
options.E: Create tunnels from both interfaces of the HA VPN gateway to the peer devices.

explanation.summary: HA VPN's SLA requires a tunnel from each of the gateway's two interfaces. HA VPN uses dynamic routing only, so a Cloud Router runs BGP on each tunnel and learns new plant subnets as they are advertised.

option_breakdown.A: Classic VPN offers a lower SLA than HA VPN, so it can't meet 99.99%.
option_breakdown.B: A single tunnel has no redundancy and doesn't qualify for the 99.99% SLA.
option_breakdown.C: Static routes need a change for every new subnet, and HA VPN tunnels use BGP rather than static routing.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. BGP through Cloud Router exchanges routes, so new subnets appear without manual changes.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Two tunnels, one per interface, is the topology the 99.99% SLA requires.

questions.title: The cheapest VMs for restartable render jobs
questions.summary: Spot VMs are the cheapest Compute Engine capacity for fault-tolerant work that can be stopped at any time; commitments suit steady usage over one or three years.
questions.question: Averill Animation renders frames for six weeks before each film release. Each job checkpoints to Cloud Storage every few minutes and can restart on any VM, and Google Cloud may reclaim VMs at any time without harm. The render farm must cost as little as possible. Which approach should you choose?

options.A: A managed instance group whose template uses the Spot provisioning model.
options.B: A three-year resource-based committed use discount for the render machines.
options.C: Standard VMs, counting on sustained use discounts over the six weeks.
options.D: Sole-tenant nodes so render VMs never share hosts with other customers.

explanation.summary: Spot VMs are heavily discounted because Compute Engine can stop them at any time. Checkpointed, restartable jobs tolerate that, and a managed instance group recreates reclaimed VMs when capacity returns.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Spot pricing is the lowest, and the group keeps the farm at size as VMs are reclaimed.
option_breakdown.B: A three-year commitment bills for capacity all year, while the farm runs only six weeks at a time.
option_breakdown.C: Sustained use discounts are far smaller than the Spot discount for interruptible work.
option_breakdown.D: Sole-tenant nodes cost more and solve an isolation requirement the stem doesn't have.

questions.title: Only the web tier may receive load balancer traffic
questions.subtopic: Secure Tags and Service Accounts in Rules
questions.summary: A firewall rule can target VMs by the service account they run as, which only people allowed to act as that account can change.
questions.question: At Quenby Insurance, web VMs run as web-sa and batch VMs as batch-sa, in the same subnet. Only the web VMs may accept TCP 443 from Google's load balancer ranges, and a developer who can edit VM network tags must not be able to extend that access to a batch VM. How should you write the allow rule's target?

options.A: Target every instance in the network, with a source of the subnet's range.
options.B: Target the web VMs' internal IP addresses as a destination range.
options.C: Target the network tag web on the web VMs.
options.D: Target the service account web-sa.

explanation.summary: Network tags can be added by anyone who can edit an instance, so they don't prove which VM is which. A target service account changes only when someone with permission to act as that account attaches it.

option_breakdown.A: Every instance would match, batch VMs included, and the source should be the load balancer ranges.
option_breakdown.B: Internal addresses change when VMs are recreated, and listing them doesn't stop a new VM taking one.
option_breakdown.C: The developer can add the web tag to a batch VM, which would open 443 on it.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Only VMs running as web-sa match, and changing a VM's service account needs actAs on the new account.

questions.title: Product images that survive a region outage within minutes
questions.summary: A dual-region Cloud Storage bucket with turbo replication replicates new objects to both regions within 15 minutes (RPO), in the two regions you choose.
questions.question: Ingleby Retail serves product images from Cloud Storage. Data must stay in two named EU regions, europe-west1 and europe-west4, and if one region fails, every image uploaded more than 15 minutes earlier must be available from the other. There should be no copy jobs to run. What should you create?

options.A: A bucket in the EU multi-region with default replication
options.B: A dual-region bucket in europe-west1 and europe-west4 with turbo replication
options.C: A regional bucket in europe-west1, copied nightly to europe-west4 by Storage Transfer Service
options.D: A regional bucket in europe-west1 with object versioning enabled

explanation.summary: Dual-region buckets keep data in exactly the two regions you choose. Turbo replication adds a 15-minute recovery point objective for newly written objects; default replication has no such target.

option_breakdown.A: The EU multi-region doesn't let you name the two regions, and default replication has no 15-minute RPO.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The bucket lives in the two named regions, and turbo replication meets the 15-minute RPO.
option_breakdown.C: A nightly copy can lose a day of uploads, and it's a job to run.
option_breakdown.D: Versioning protects against overwrites and deletions, not against the loss of a region.

questions.title: Paying per Pod with no nodes to manage
questions.summary: GKE Autopilot manages nodes and bills for the Pods' resource requests, so the team sets requests and nothing else.
questions.question: Brisco Health's small platform team wants to run about forty containerised services on Kubernetes. They don't want to choose machine types, size node pools or patch nodes, and they want to pay for the CPU and memory their Pods request rather than for idle node capacity. Which option should you choose?

options.A: A GKE Standard cluster with the cluster autoscaler enabled
options.B: Self-managed Kubernetes on a managed instance group
options.C: A GKE Autopilot cluster
options.D: A GKE Standard cluster with node auto-provisioning on Spot VMs

explanation.summary: In Autopilot, Google provisions and manages the nodes, and you pay for the resources your Pods request. Standard clusters bill for the nodes, used or idle, and the team manages them.

option_breakdown.A: The autoscaler resizes node pools, but the team still picks machine types and pays for whole nodes.
option_breakdown.B: Self-managed Kubernetes adds control plane and node management, the opposite of what the team wants.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. No node management, and billing follows Pod resource requests.
option_breakdown.D: Auto-provisioning creates node pools, but billing is still per node, and the team owns the configuration.

questions.title: Orders kept while the consumer is down for hours
questions.summary: Pub/Sub decouples producers and consumers and retains unacknowledged messages in a subscription for up to seven days by default.
questions.question: At Tarrant Outfitters, the storefront sends each order to a fulfilment service that is sometimes down for maintenance for up to six hours. No order may be lost, the storefront must not slow down while fulfilment is down, and fulfilment should catch up afterwards. What should you use between them?

options.A: A Pub/Sub topic with a pull subscription for the fulfilment service
options.B: Direct HTTPS calls from the storefront, retried until fulfilment answers
options.C: A Cloud SQL table that fulfilment polls every minute
options.D: A shared Filestore directory where the storefront writes one file per order

explanation.summary: Pub/Sub accepts messages whether or not subscribers are running, and keeps unacknowledged messages in the subscription for seven days by default. The consumer pulls the backlog when it returns.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Publishing is quick and independent of the consumer, and the backlog waits in the subscription.
option_breakdown.B: Retrying synchronously ties the storefront to fulfilment's downtime and slows checkout.
option_breakdown.C: A polled table works but adds a database to run and scale for what is a messaging job.
option_breakdown.D: Files on a shared directory need their own locking and clean-up and give no delivery guarantees.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud pubsub topics create orders
gcloud pubsub subscriptions create fulfilment --topic=orders --ack-deadline=60

questions.title: Processing each upload as it arrives
questions.summary: An Eventarc trigger on Cloud Storage's object-finalized event delivers each new object to a Cloud Run service, with no polling.
questions.question: Customers of Pellow Insurance upload claim photos to a Cloud Storage bucket. Each new photo must be resized within seconds of upload by a containerised service, with no servers to manage and nothing that polls the bucket. What should you set up?

options.A: A Cloud Scheduler job that runs a Cloud Run job every minute to list new objects
options.B: An object lifecycle rule that runs the resizer when an object is created
options.C: A Compute Engine VM that watches the bucket with gcloud storage ls in a loop
options.D: A Cloud Run service with an Eventarc trigger for the bucket's object-finalized events

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage emits an object-finalized event when an upload completes. Eventarc routes it to a Cloud Run service, which scales with the uploads and runs only when there is work.

option_breakdown.A: Listing every minute is polling, and it adds up to a minute of delay.
option_breakdown.B: Lifecycle rules only change storage classes or delete objects; they can't run code.
option_breakdown.C: A watching VM is a server to manage, and the loop is polling.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Each finished upload triggers the service within seconds, with no servers and no polling.

questions.title: UDP game traffic that must keep client addresses
questions.summary: An external passthrough Network Load Balancer handles UDP and preserves client source IPs, so backend firewall rules must admit the clients' addresses.
questions.question: Dunmore Games runs UDP game servers on port 7777 in one region, on a managed instance group. Players connect from the internet, and the servers must see each player's real IP address. The VPC currently allows only health-check traffic to the servers. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Allow ingress on UDP 7777 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the game servers.
options.B: Create an external passthrough Network Load Balancer for UDP 7777 with the group as its backend.
options.C: Create an external proxy Network Load Balancer for the game servers.
options.D: Create a Cloud NAT gateway for the game servers' subnet.
options.E: Create a global external Application Load Balancer for the game servers.

explanation.summary: A passthrough Network Load Balancer forwards packets without proxying, so UDP works and the source IP is the player's. Because packets keep the client source, the backends' firewall must allow the players' traffic, not just the load balancer's.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Passthrough traffic arrives from players' addresses, so the rule must admit them on UDP 7777.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. It supports UDP and preserves each player's IP address.
option_breakdown.C: Proxy Network Load Balancers terminate TCP and don't carry UDP, and the backends would see the proxy's address.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud NAT handles outbound connections from private VMs, not inbound players.
option_breakdown.E: Application Load Balancers handle HTTP(S), not raw UDP.

questions.title: An API used only in office hours
questions.summary: Cloud Run runs stateless containers, scales to zero when idle and bills for the time requests are processed by default.
questions.question: Hartwell Surveyors has a stateless HTTP API in a container. It gets traffic only from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, sometimes in bursts of 200 requests a second, and none at night or weekends. The team wants no servers to manage and to pay nothing while there is no traffic. Which platform should you choose?

options.A: A single large Compute Engine VM on a schedule
options.B: A Compute Engine managed instance group with autoscaling
options.C: Cloud Run, with the minimum number of instances at zero
options.D: A GKE Standard cluster with the cluster autoscaler

explanation.summary: Cloud Run scales container instances with requests, down to zero when there are none, and with the default request-based billing charges only while requests are being handled.

option_breakdown.A: One VM is a server to manage, and it may not handle the bursts.
option_breakdown.B: A managed instance group keeps at least one VM running and is a fleet to manage.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. It handles the bursts, costs nothing when idle and has no servers to manage.
option_breakdown.D: Standard clusters bill for nodes even when idle, and nodes are the team's to manage.

questions.title: Two teams' VPCs talking over private addresses
questions.summary: VPC Network Peering connects two VPCs over internal IPs while each team keeps its own administration; firewall rules in each VPC still decide what's allowed.
questions.question: At Bramley Labs, the analytics VPC (10.10.0.0/16) in one project must reach a PostgreSQL VM in the research VPC (10.20.0.0/16) in another project, on TCP 5432 over internal IPs. Each team must keep administering its own VPC, and the research VPC has only rules for its own traffic. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: In the research VPC, allow ingress on TCP 5432 from 10.10.0.0/16 to the database VM.
options.B: Give the database VM an external IP and allow 5432 from the internet.
options.C: Create a VPC Network Peering connection from each VPC to the other.
options.D: Move both projects into one Shared VPC host project.
options.E: Create Cloud NAT in the analytics VPC so its VMs reach the research VPC.

explanation.summary: Peering exchanges subnet routes between the two VPCs once both sides create it, and each VPC stays separately administered. Peering doesn't open any traffic: the research VPC still needs an ingress rule for the analytics range.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The implied deny ingress rule blocks peered traffic until a rule allows it.
option_breakdown.B: An external IP sends the traffic over the internet, not over internal IPs.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Peering needs a connection created from each side, and then the subnet routes are exchanged.
option_breakdown.D: Shared VPC puts the network under one host project, so the teams would no longer administer their own VPCs.
option_breakdown.E: Cloud NAT is for outbound internet access, not for traffic between VPCs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings create analytics-to-research --network=analytics \
  --peer-project=RESEARCH_PROJECT --peer-network=research

questions.title: An Eventarc trigger for new uploads that fails to create
questions.summary: Eventarc triggers for Cloud Storage events need the project's Cloud Storage service agent to hold Pub/Sub Publisher, because Cloud Storage publishes the events through Pub/Sub.
questions.question: You deployed a Cloud Run service that must process every image uploaded to the bucket intake-photos. When you create an Eventarc trigger for the object finalized event of that bucket, creation fails with a Pub/Sub permission error. You want to follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the project's Cloud Storage service agent the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the project.
options.B: Grant your own user account the Pub/Sub Admin role on the project, and create the trigger again.
options.C: Grant the Eventarc service agent the Storage Admin role on the intake-photos bucket.
options.D: Grant the Compute Engine default service account the Editor role on the project.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage delivers its events to Eventarc through Pub/Sub, and it publishes as the project's Cloud Storage service agent. That agent needs the Pub/Sub Publisher role before a Cloud Storage trigger can be created.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The Cloud Storage service agent publishes the bucket's events to Pub/Sub, so it needs Pub/Sub Publisher.
option_breakdown.B: The error is about the identity that publishes the events, not about you, so a role on your own account doesn't fix it.
option_breakdown.C: The Eventarc agent doesn't need to manage the bucket, and Storage Admin is far broader than anything the trigger needs.
option_breakdown.D: Editor on the default compute account is over-broad and is not the identity that publishes Cloud Storage events.

questions.title: A Cloud SQL database that must survive a region outage
questions.summary: Cloud SQL HA protects against a zone failure only. For a region failure with a small RPO, add a cross-region read replica and promote it.
questions.question: Your Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in us-east4 is configured for high availability. The business now requires that the database can serve again within 30 minutes if the whole region becomes unavailable, losing at most a few minutes of data. You want to minimize cost and operational effort. What should you do?

options.A: Rely on the existing high availability configuration, which fails over to a standby in another region.
options.B: Export the database to a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket every night, and import it after a failure.
options.C: Create a cross-region read replica in another region, and promote it if us-east4 becomes unavailable.
options.D: Run a second primary instance in another region, and have the application write to both instances.

explanation.summary: A cross-region read replica is kept current by asynchronous replication, so promoting it in another region loses only the last moments of writes and takes minutes.

option_breakdown.A: The HA standby is in another zone of the same region, so a region outage takes both instances down.
option_breakdown.B: A nightly export can lose up to a day of data, and importing a large database takes far longer than 30 minutes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The replica lags by seconds to minutes, and promotion turns it into a standalone primary quickly.
option_breakdown.D: Dual writes from the application are fragile, hard to keep consistent, and double the cost of the primary.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud sql instances create orders-dr --master-instance-name=orders --region=us-west1
gcloud sql instances promote-replica orders-dr   # only during a regional outage

questions.title: On-premises servers reaching only VPC-SC supported APIs
questions.summary: For on-premises access to Google APIs over Interconnect or VPN, advertise the VIP range from Cloud Router and point DNS at it; restricted.googleapis.com (199.36.153.4/30) reaches only APIs supported by VPC Service Controls.
questions.question: Servers in your data center reach your VPC over Cloud Interconnect and have no internet access. They must read objects in Cloud Storage over the Interconnect, and the security team requires that only APIs supported by VPC Service Controls can be reached this way. What should you do?

options.A: Enable Private Google Access on the subnets in the region of the Interconnect attachments.
options.B: Create a Cloud NAT gateway in the region of the Interconnect that translates the on-premises ranges.
options.C: Advertise 199.36.153.4/30 from the Cloud Router, and resolve googleapis.com to restricted.googleapis.com on premises.
options.D: Advertise 199.36.153.8/30 from the Cloud Router, and resolve googleapis.com to private.googleapis.com on premises.

explanation.summary: On-premises hosts reach Google APIs privately when Cloud Router advertises the VIP range and on-premises DNS maps the API domains to it. The restricted VIP, 199.36.153.4/30, only serves APIs that VPC Service Controls supports.

option_breakdown.A: Private Google Access applies to VMs in those subnets, not to hosts on premises.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud NAT translates traffic from Google Cloud resources; it doesn't serve on-premises hosts.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The restricted VIP is reachable over the Interconnect and only serves VPC Service Controls supported APIs.
option_breakdown.D: The private VIP works over the Interconnect but serves most Google APIs, not only the supported ones.

questions.title: Cloud Run reaching a private Memorystore instance cheaply
questions.summary: Direct VPC egress gives a Cloud Run service an address in a VPC subnet with no connector instances to run or pay for.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service must use a Memorystore for Redis instance that has only a private IP address in the VPC prod-vpc. You want the lowest cost and no extra VMs or connector instances to manage. What should you do?

options.A: Create a Serverless VPC Access connector in prod-vpc and attach it to the service.
options.B: Configure Direct VPC egress on the Cloud Run service to a subnet of prod-vpc.
options.C: Assign an external IP address to the Memorystore instance and restrict it with a firewall rule.
options.D: Create a Cloud NAT gateway in prod-vpc so that the service can reach the instance's address.

explanation.summary: With Direct VPC egress, Cloud Run instances get IP addresses from a subnet you choose and send traffic straight into the VPC, so there is no connector to provision or pay for. Plan the subnet's size for the instances it must hold.

option_breakdown.A: A connector works, but it runs instances you pay for and manage, which the stem wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Traffic goes straight into the VPC from the service's instances, with no connector VMs.
option_breakdown.C: Memorystore instances have private addresses only; they can't take an external IP.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud NAT gives VPC resources outbound internet access; it gives Cloud Run no path into the VPC.

questions.title: Rolling a new image without losing capacity
questions.summary: A proactive rolling update with max unavailable 0 adds new VMs before removing old ones; a regional MIG needs max surge of at least the number of zones.
questions.question: A regional managed instance group of 9 VMs serves production traffic. You created a new instance template that uses a patched image. Serving capacity must never fall below 9 VMs during the rollout, and VMs must be replaced automatically. What should you do?

options.A: Set the new template on the group, and then delete the old VMs one at a time by hand.
options.B: Start a proactive rolling update to the new template with max unavailable 0 and max surge 3.
options.C: Start an opportunistic update to the new template with max unavailable set to 0.
options.D: Create a second group from the new template, and delete the old group when it is healthy.

explanation.summary: With max unavailable 0, the group creates surge VMs from the new template and removes old VMs only when the new ones are running. A regional group spreads the surge across its zones, so max surge must be at least 3.

option_breakdown.A: Manual deletion lowers capacity each time a VM is deleted, and the replacement isn't automatic.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. New VMs are added before old ones go, so capacity never drops, and the group replaces every VM.
option_breakdown.C: An opportunistic update applies only when VMs are recreated for other reasons, so nothing is replaced now.
option_breakdown.D: A second group works, but it means rewiring the load balancer and cleaning up by hand.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig \
  --region=us-central1 --version=template=web-v2 --max-unavailable=0 --max-surge=3

questions.title: No GKE upgrades during a sales freeze
questions.summary: A maintenance exclusion with the scope 'no minor or node upgrades' blocks minor and node upgrades for the period while still allowing control plane patches.
questions.question: Your production GKE Standard cluster is enrolled in the Regular release channel. During a two-week holiday sales period, no minor version upgrades and no node upgrades may happen, but security patches to the control plane are acceptable. What should you do?

options.A: Unenroll the cluster from the Regular release channel for the two weeks.
options.B: Set a recurring maintenance window that starts after the sales period ends.
options.C: Add a maintenance exclusion with the scope no minor or node upgrades.
options.D: Disable node auto-upgrade on every node pool, and re-enable it afterwards.

explanation.summary: Maintenance exclusions block automatic upgrades for a period. The scope 'no minor or node upgrades' stops minor and node pool upgrades but still lets GKE apply control plane patches.

option_breakdown.A: Changing channels is disruptive, and leaving a channel changes how the cluster is upgraded afterwards.
option_breakdown.B: A maintenance window only says when maintenance may happen; it repeats and doesn't block a period.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The exclusion covers exactly the sales period and still allows control plane patches.
option_breakdown.D: Clusters enrolled in a release channel can't turn off node auto-upgrade.

questions.title: Dead-lettered messages that never arrive
questions.summary: Dead-lettering is done by the Pub/Sub service agent, which needs Publisher on the dead-letter topic and Subscriber on the source subscription.
questions.question: A Pub/Sub subscriber keeps failing on a few malformed messages, which are redelivered endlessly. You configured the subscription to forward a message to the topic orders-dead after 5 delivery attempts, but no messages ever reach orders-dead. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Raise the subscription's acknowledgement deadline to its maximum of 600 seconds.
options.B: Grant the Pub/Sub service agent the Pub/Sub Subscriber role on the original subscription.
options.C: Grant the subscriber application's service account the Pub/Sub Admin role on the project.
options.D: Enable message ordering on the original subscription.
options.E: Grant the Pub/Sub service agent the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the orders-dead topic.

explanation.summary: Pub/Sub forwards undeliverable messages as its own service agent. That agent must be able to publish to the dead-letter topic and to acknowledge, as a subscriber, the messages on the source subscription.

option_breakdown.A: A longer deadline only delays redelivery; malformed messages still fail every time.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The service agent removes the forwarded message from the source subscription, which needs Subscriber.
option_breakdown.C: The application doesn't forward dead-lettered messages, and Admin is far broader than anything needed.
option_breakdown.D: Ordering changes delivery order; it has nothing to do with dead-lettering.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Without Publisher on orders-dead, the service agent can't forward any message there.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud pubsub topics add-iam-policy-binding orders-dead \
  --member=serviceAccount:service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/pubsub.publisher
gcloud pubsub subscriptions add-iam-policy-binding orders-sub \
  --member=serviceAccount:service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/pubsub.subscriber

questions.title: A peered VPC sharing the hub's VPN to on-premises
questions.summary: Peered VPCs can use a hub's hybrid connection when the hub exports custom routes and the spoke imports them, and the hub's Cloud Router advertises the spoke's ranges to on-premises.
questions.question: The VPC hub-vpc connects to on-premises through HA VPN and a Cloud Router. The VPC app-vpc is peered with hub-vpc. VMs in app-vpc must reach on-premises, and on-premises must reach app-vpc, without creating a second VPN. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Peer app-vpc directly with the on-premises network over the existing VPN.
options.B: Enable global dynamic routing on app-vpc so that it learns the on-premises routes.
options.C: Configure the Cloud Router to advertise app-vpc's subnet ranges as custom advertised routes.
options.D: Create static routes in app-vpc whose next hop is the HA VPN tunnel in hub-vpc, one for each on-premises range.
options.E: Export custom routes on hub-vpc's side of the peering, and import them on app-vpc's side.

explanation.summary: The dynamic routes that hub-vpc learns from on-premises reach app-vpc only if custom routes are exported and imported over the peering. On-premises learns app-vpc's ranges only if the Cloud Router advertises them, because by default it advertises only its own VPC's subnets.

option_breakdown.A: VPC Network Peering connects Google Cloud VPC networks only, never an on-premises network.
option_breakdown.B: app-vpc has no Cloud Router of its own; its routing mode doesn't import the peer's routes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Custom advertisements tell on-premises how to reach app-vpc through the VPN.
option_breakdown.D: A static route's next hop must be in the same VPC, so app-vpc can't point at hub-vpc's tunnel.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Exporting and importing custom routes shares the on-premises routes with app-vpc.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings update hub-to-app --network=hub-vpc --export-custom-routes
gcloud compute networks peerings update app-to-hub --network=app-vpc --import-custom-routes
gcloud compute routers update hub-router --region=us-central1 --advertisement-mode=custom \
  --set-advertisement-groups=all_subnets --set-advertisement-ranges=10.20.0.0/16

questions.title: Pub/Sub events into BigQuery with no pipeline code
questions.summary: A BigQuery subscription writes each Pub/Sub message straight into a table, with no Dataflow job or code; the Pub/Sub service agent needs write access to the table.
questions.question: Click events are published to the Pub/Sub topic clicks as JSON whose fields match the columns of a BigQuery table. Analysts need each event to be queryable in BigQuery within a minute. You want to minimize operational overhead and custom code. What should you do?

options.A: Run a Dataflow streaming job from a Google template that reads the topic and writes to the table.
options.B: Write a Cloud Run service that receives push messages and inserts rows with the streaming API.
options.C: Create a BigQuery subscription on the topic that writes to the table, using the table's schema.
options.D: Create a Cloud Storage subscription on the topic, and load its files into BigQuery every hour.

explanation.summary: A BigQuery subscription writes messages into the table as they arrive, mapping JSON fields to columns when it uses the table schema. There is nothing to run or code; the Pub/Sub service agent needs BigQuery Data Editor on the table.

option_breakdown.A: A template avoids writing code, but a streaming Dataflow job is still workers to run and pay for.
option_breakdown.B: A custom service is code to write, deploy and maintain, which the stem wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Pub/Sub writes to BigQuery itself, so there is no job, service or code to operate.
option_breakdown.D: Hourly loads miss the one-minute requirement and add a scheduled job to maintain.

questions.title: Monthly OS patching with a compliance report
questions.summary: VM Manager's patch deployments apply OS patches on a schedule, and its patch compliance reporting shows which VMs are missing patches.
questions.question: Your project has 300 Linux VMs. The security team requires that OS patches are applied every month during a maintenance window, and wants a report of which VMs are missing patches. You want to minimize custom scripting. What should you do?

options.A: Add a startup script to every VM that runs the package manager's upgrade command at boot.
options.B: Rebuild every VM each month from the newest public image with a Cloud Build pipeline.
options.C: Enable VM Manager for the VMs, and create a monthly patch deployment that targets them.
options.D: Turn on automatic restart for every VM so that the guest OS installs updates as it boots.

explanation.summary: With VM Manager enabled, the OS Config agent on each VM reports its state. A patch deployment applies patches on a schedule inside a window, and patch compliance shows which VMs still need patches.

option_breakdown.A: A startup script only runs at boot, gives no schedule or window, and produces no compliance report.
option_breakdown.B: Rebuilding 300 VMs every month is heavy, risky automation, and still gives no compliance view.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Scheduled patch deployments and compliance reporting are built in, with no scripts.
option_breakdown.D: Automatic restart brings a VM back after a crash; it doesn't install anything.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute os-config patch-deployments create monthly-linux --file=monthly.yaml
# monthly.yaml: instanceFilter: all, recurringSchedule: monthly, duration: 4h

questions.title: Cutting egress cost for users in one country
questions.summary: Standard Tier egress costs less but works only with regional resources: a regional external load balancer and a regional Standard Tier address.
questions.question: A video service runs in europe-west3, and all of its users are in Germany. Internet egress is the largest item on the bill. You want to reduce egress cost, and you accept that traffic travels further over the public internet. Which setup should you use?

options.A: A regional external Application Load Balancer with a Standard Tier regional address.
options.B: A global external Application Load Balancer in the Premium Tier, the default tier.
options.C: A global external Application Load Balancer with a Standard Tier global address.
options.D: A cross-region internal Application Load Balancer with a Premium Tier address.

explanation.summary: Standard Tier hands traffic to the internet close to the region, which costs less than Premium Tier's Google backbone. It's regional only, so it needs a regional load balancer and a regional address.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A regional load balancer can use a Standard Tier address, the cheaper egress option.
option_breakdown.B: Premium Tier carries traffic on Google's network, which is faster but costs more for egress.
option_breakdown.C: Global load balancers require Premium Tier; there are no Standard Tier global addresses.
option_breakdown.D: An internal load balancer isn't reachable from the internet at all.
